stem_md:
consider  $n\geq 6$  points  $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$  on the plane such that no three of them are colinear. We call graph with vertices  $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$  a "road network" if it is connected, each edge is a line segment, and no two edges intersect each other at points other than the vertices. Prove that there are three road networks  $G_1,G_2,G_3$  such that  $G_i$  and  $G_j$  don't have a common edge for  $1\leq i,j\leq 3$ .

Proposed by Morteza Saghafian
solution_md:
For convenience rename the points  $P_1,...,P_n$ .
We will proceed by induction on  $n$ , starting from  $n=6$ .
By induction, it easy to see that we can construct by adding  $P_{i+1}$  (if necessary relabel the points so that we have the right order) outside of the convex hull of  $P_1...P_i$ .
So we may assume  $P_n$  is outside the convex hull of  $P_1...P_{n-1}$  [name this convex hull  $\mathcal{P}$  for convenience.
Since  $P_n$  is outside  $\mathcal{P}$  there exist at least two points (say  $P_1,P_2$ ) such that the segments  $P_1P_n$  and  $P_2P_n$  which don't intersect  $\mathcal{P}$ . If there also exists a third such point  $P_3$ , simply add one of these three segments to each of the three networks.
Otherwise, assume wlog that road network  $G_1$  didn't have  $P_1P_2$  as a road. Now, consider the process of smoothly rotating the ray  $P_nP_1$  to the ray  $P_nP_2$  (passing through every other vertex in the process). Let wlog  $P_3$  be (one of) the vertex connected to  $P_1$  inside  $G_1$  (by hypothesis this point couldn't have been  $P_2$ ). If  $P_nP_3$  is uninterrupted by other roads in  $G_1$ , just add this segment. Otherwise, in the process of rotation, let  $P_4$  be first "obstacle" to seeing segment  $P_1P_3$ . It is clear to see that adding point  $P_nP_4$  will work, as there can't be any ther obstacle (since  $P_4$  was the first and no tree points are aligned).
Now, since  $P_nP_1$ , $P_nP_2$ , and  $P_nP_4$  are distinct, we can just add these three to  $G_2,G_3,G_1$  respectively, and we are done.
So it suffices to check  $n=6$  which has just a finite amount of cases.

We call an infinite set  $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$  good if for all parwise different integers  $a,b,c\in S$ , all positive divisors of  $\frac{a^c-b^c}{a-b}$  are in  $S$ . for all positive integers  $n>1$ , prove that there exists a good set  $S$  such that  $n \not \in S$ .

Proposed by Seyed Reza Hosseini Dolatabadi
solution_md: Let  $p$  be a prime divisor of  $n$  and pick  $S$  to be the set of all numbers with all prime factors  $> p$ . This works, since no prime at most  $p$  can divide  $\frac{a^c - b^c}{a-b}$ . Suppose not, and say  $q$  divided it, then  $a^c \equiv b^c \pmod q$ , write  $a \equiv g^{m} \pmod q$  and  $b = g^{n} \pmod q$  for some primitive root  $g$ , then we have  $cm \equiv cn \pmod {q-1}$ , but since  $c$  is coprime to  $p-1$ , we must have  $m \equiv n \pmod {p-1}$  and so in fact,  $q | a-b$ , but then  $v_q(a^c - b^c) = v_q(a-b) + v_q(c) = v_q(a-b)$  so  $\frac{a^c - b^c}{a-b}$  is not divisible by  $q$ . Finally, since  $n$  does have a prime factor at most  $p$ , it is not in  $S$ , so we are done.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Consider a table with  $n$  rows and  $2n$  columns. we put some blocks in some of the cells. After putting blocks in the table we put a robot on a cell and it starts moving in one of the directions right, left, down or up. It can change the direction only when it reaches a block or border. Find the smallest number  $m$  such that we can put  $m$  blocks on the table and choose a starting point for the robot so it can visit all of the unblocked cells. (the robot can't enter the blocked cells.)

Proposed by Seyed Mohammad Seyedjavadi and Alireza Tavakoli
solution_md:
Solved with **rama1728**.

We claim that the answer is  $\lfloor{\frac{n}{2}\rfloor} -1$ . Say we have a working configuration with  $m$  blocks on it. One can notice that the robot can slide along a row if and only if there is a block or an edge above or below it. Thus, placing a block 'unlocks' two rows. From this we can note that, we require, 
\[2m +3 \geq n \implies m \geq \lfloor{\frac{n}{2}\rfloor} -1\]
Now, we shall give a construction to show that this number of blocks is sufficient.
Note that, when  $n \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ , we can simply place blocks on rows  $3,7,11,\dots$  in the left-most column and rows  $6,10,\dots$  of the right-most columns and simply start from the third row. For all other  $n$ , simply place blocks on the left-most column on rows  $5,9,13,\dots$  and on the right-most column for rows  $4,8,12,\dots$  and begin on the second row.

Thus, indeed our answer is correct and we are done.

solution_md: By considering directed angles (mod 180), it is easy to note that  $ \angle RAQ \equal{} \angle BPC \equal{} \alpha,$    $ \angle BQA \equal{} \angle APB \equal{} \gamma$  and  $ \angle ARC \equal{} \angle APC \equal{} \beta.$  Therefore,  $ \angle AQB \equal{} \angle AHB$  and  $ \angle ARC \equal{} \angle AHC$   $ \Longrightarrow$  quadrilaterals  $ AQBH$  and  $ ARCH$  are both cyclic. Hence $ \angle ARX \equiv \angle ARH \equal{} \angle ACH \equal{} 90^{\circ} \minus{} \alpha$   $ \Longrightarrow  \angle AXR \equal{} \angle QAR \plus{} \angle ARX \equal{} \alpha \plus{} 90^{\circ} \minus{} \alpha \equal{} 90^{\circ} \equal{} \angle AEH$   $ \Longrightarrow$  quadrilateral  $ AXEH$  is cyclic, which yields  $ \angle AHX \equiv \angle AHR \equal{} \angle ACR \equal{} \angle AEX$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $ EX\parallel RC \parallel AP.$

stem_md: Let  $n$  and  $k$  be two positive integers. Prove that there exist infinitely many perfect squares of the form  $n \cdot 2^k - 7$ .
solution_md:
The problem is this: "For each $k\in\mathbb {N}$ , there always exists positive integer $n$ such that $n.2^k-7$ is a perfect square
Now this is what I call a fantastic NT problem. We shall induct on $k $ . For $k=1,2,3$ , the result is fairly obvious. Now let the result be true for some $k $ , i.e., $\exists a,n\in\mathbb {N} $ such that $a^2=n2^k-7$ . If $n $ is even then $a^2=\left (\frac {n}{2}\right)2^{k+1}-7$ does the job for $(k+1) $ . Suppose $n $ is odd. So we basically want some $b\in\mathbb {N} $ such that $b^2=n'2^{k+1}-7\iff b^2-a^2=2^k\times$ some odd number, i.e., $v_2 (b^2-a^2)=k\implies v_2 (b-a)+v_2 (b+a)=k $ . Clearly both $a $ and $b $ are odd. Since $\gcd (b-a,b+a)=2\gcd (a,b)\implies v_2 (\gcd (a-b,a+b))=1\implies v_2 (x)=1$ is satisfied for atleast one of $(b-a),(b+a) $ . Suppose $v_2 (a+b)=1\implies v_2 (a-b)=(k-1) $ . Simply set $a-b=2^{k-1} $ and observe that $v_2 (a+b)=v_2 (2b+2^{k-1})=2\forall k>3$ as $b $ is odd. Hence all requirements are met and induction is complete. NOTE : This method also proves the following stronger problem. For any fixed $k\in\mathbb {N} $ , there exist infinitely many $n\in\mathbb {N} $ such that $n2^k-7$ is a perfect square.

stem_md:
Let  $ABC$  be an acute angled triangle,  $O$  be the circumcenter of  $ABC$ , and  $R$  be the cicumradius.  $AO$  meets the circumcircle of  $BOC$  at  $A'$ ,  $BO$  meets the circumcircle of  $COA$ , and  $CO$  meets the circumcircle of  $AOB$  at  $C'$ . Prove that
\[OA' \cdot OB' \cdot OC' \geq 8R^3.\]
When does inequality occur?
solution_md:
Let  $\alpha$ ,  $\beta$ ,  $\gamma$  be  $\angle A$ ,  $\angle B$ ,  $\angle C$  respectively.
Using ***Ptolemy*** for  $~$   $\square AOCB'$  , we get  $~$   $OB'=\frac{AB'+CB'}{CA}\cdot R=\frac{\sin 2\gamma+\sin 2\alpha}{\sin 2\beta}\cdot R$ Let  $x$ ,  $y$ ,  $z$  be  $~$   $\sin 2\alpha$ ,  $~$   $\sin 2\beta$ ,  $~$   $\sin 2\gamma$  respectively. $\therefore OA'\cdot OB'\cdot OC'=\frac{(y+z)(z+x)(x+y)}{xyz}R^{3}\geq 8R^{3}$  , by ***AM-GM*** *inequality*

stem_md: Two circles  $O, O'$  meet each other at points  $A, B$ . A line from  $A$  intersects the circle  $O$  at  $C$  and the circle  $O'$  at  $D$  ( $A$  is between  $C$  and  $D$ ). Let  $M,N$  be the midpoints of the arcs  $BC, BD$ , respectively (not containing  $A$ ), and let  $K$  be the midpoint of the segment  $CD$ . Show that  $\angle KMN = 90^\circ$ .
solution_md: Let  $B'$  be the inverse of  $B$  under the inversion with center  $A$  and power  $\overline{AC} \cdot \overline{AD}.$  Circles  $(O),(O')$  go to lines  $DB'$  and  $CB'$   $\Longrightarrow$   $M' \equiv AM \cap DB'$  and  $N' \equiv AN \cap CB'$  are the inverses of  $M,N,$  respectively. Let  $U \equiv M'N' \cap CD.$  Since the pencil  $A(C,B,M,N)$  is harmonic, it follows that pencil  $B'(M',N',A,U)$  is also harmonic  $\Longrightarrow$   $(C,D,A,U)$  is harmonic  $\Longrightarrow$   $\overline{AC} \cdot \overline{AD}=\overline{AK} \cdot \overline{AU},$  i.e.  $U$  is the inverse of  $A$  under the referred inversion. Since  $U,M',N'$  are collinear, then  $K,$   $M,$   $N,$   $A$  are concyclic and the conclusion follows.

stem_md: Let  $f : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N$  be an injective function such that there exists a positive integer  $k$  for which  $f(n) \leq n^k$ . Prove that there exist infinitely many primes  $q$  such that the equation  $f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod q$  has a solution in prime numbers.
solution_md:
Arguing by contradiction, suppose the claim is not true. In that case there exists a finite set of primes  $p_1,p_2,\dots, p_m$ , such that for any  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , it holds:
\[f(n)=p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}\dots p_m^{a_m}.\]
Fix some big  $N\in \mathbb{N}$ . For  $n\in [N,2N]$ , we have:
\[f(n)\leq 2^kN^k \]
which implies:
\[a_i\leq \log (2^k N^k)=k+k\log N< 2k\log N\,,\, i=1,2,\dots,m\]
Hence, all possible values of  $f(n)$ , when  $N\leq n \leq 2N$  are at most  $(2k\log N)^m$ Since  $f$  is an injection, it must hold:
\[N\leq (2k\log N)^m\]
But it doesn't hold when  $N$  is sufficiently large, a contradiction.

Let  $f: \mathbb R \to\mathbb R$  be a function such that  $|f(x)| \leq 1$  for all  $x \in \mathbb R$  and
\[f \left( x + \frac{13}{42} \right) + f(x) = f \left( x + \frac 17 \right) + f \left( x + \frac 16 \right), \quad \forall x \in \mathbb R.\]
Show that  $f$  is a periodic function.
solution_md:
Let $f: \mathbb R \to\mathbb R$ be a function such that $|f(x)| \leq 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb R$ and \[f \left( x + \frac{13}{42} \right) + f(x) = f \left( x + \frac 17 \right) + f \left( x + \frac 16 \right), \quad \forall x \in \mathbb R.\] Show that $f$ is a periodic function.
solutionfor simplicity, denote $g(x):= f(\frac x{42})$ . Then we have $g(x)-g(x+6)=g(x+7)-g(x+13)$ , iterating this $\implies g(x)-g(x+6)=g(x+42)-g(x+48)$ . We also have $g(x)-g(x+7)=g(x+6)-g(x+13)$ , iterating this $\implies g(x)-g(x+7)=g(x+42)-g(x+49)$ . So, putting $y=x-6$ , we have $g(y)-g(y+1)=g(y+42)-g(y+43)$ . Summing this up for $y,y+1,...,y+42$ yields $g(y)-g(y+42)=g(y+42)-g(y+84)$ .. Now suppose $g(y)\ne g(y-42)$ . Then by iterating this, we see that $g$ and thus $f$ cannot be bounded, contradiction to $|f|\le 1$ . So $f$ has period $1$ .

stem_md:
Let  $\omega_1,\omega_2, . . . ,\omega_k$  be distinct real numbers with a nonzero sum. Prove that there exist integers  $n_1, n_2, . . . , n_k$  such that  $\sum_{i=1}^k n_i\omega_i>0$ , and for any non-identical permutation  $\pi$  of  $\{1, 2,\dots, k\}$  we have
\[\sum_{i=1}^k n_i\omega_{\pi(i)}<0.\]
solution_md:
Without loss of generality, let  $\omega_1 > \omega_2 > \ldots > \omega_k$ , and let  $S = \omega_1 + \omega_2 + \ldots + \omega_k$ . It is clear that of all sums of the form  $2 \omega_{\pi(1)} + \omega_{\pi(2)} + \ldots + \omega_{\pi(n)}$ ,  $2\omega_1 + \omega_2 + \ldots + \omega_n$  is greatest and  $\omega_1 + 2\omega_2 + \omega_3 + \ldots + \omega_n$  is the second greatest. Because the rationals are dense over the reals, we can find some rational number  $\epsilon = \frac{a}{b}, b>0$  such that 
 \[ \omega_1 + 2\omega_2 + \ldots + \omega_n + S \epsilon < 0 < 2\omega_1 + \omega_2 + \ldots + \omega_n + S \epsilon\]
Then 
\begin{align*}
(2+\epsilon)\omega_1 + (1+\epsilon)\omega_2 + \ldots + \omega_n 
&> 0 > (1 + \epsilon)\omega_1 + (2+\epsilon)\omega_2 + (1+\epsilon)\omega_3 + \ldots + (1+\epsilon)\omega_n  
&\geq (2+\epsilon)\omega_{\pi(1)} + (1+\epsilon)\omega_{\pi(2)} + \ldots + (1+\epsilon)\omega_{\pi(n)} \end{align*}
for any permutation  $\pi$  distinct from the identity. Multiplying both sides by  $b$  shows that the sequence  $n_1 = 2b + a = b(2 + \epsilon)$  and  $n_i = b + a = b(1 + \epsilon)$  for  $2 \leq i \leq k$  suffices.

stem_md:
Let  $ G$  be a simple graph. Suppose that size of largest independent set in  $ G$  is  $ \alpha$ . Prove that:
a) Vertices of  $ G$  can be partitioned to at most  $ \alpha$  paths.
b) Suppose that a vertex and an edge are also cycles. Prove that vertices of  $ G$  can be partitioned to at most  $ \alpha$  cycles.
solution_md:
a) Consider a path partition of  $G$  with minimal cardinality  $p$ . Let  $P_i = v_{i,1}v_{i,2}\ldots v_{i,\ell_i}$  for  $1\leq i \leq p$ . Clearly  $v_{i,1}v_{j,1}$  is not an edge for any  $1\leq i \neq j \leq p$  (or else we can "glue" the two paths  $P_i$  and  $P_j$ ). Therefore the set  $\{v_{i,1} \mid 1\leq i \leq p\}$  is an independent set, and so  $p\leq \alpha$ .
The result remains true for digraphs; it's the Gallai-Milgram theorem (with a more arduous proof).

b) This is a theorem of Lajos Pósa.

stem_md:
Let  $ A\equal{}\{A_1,\dots,A_m\}$  be a family distinct subsets of  $ \{1,2,\dots,n\}$  with at most  $ \frac n2$  elements. Assume that  $ A_i\not\subset A_j$  and  $ A_i\cap A_j\neq\emptyset$  for each  $ i,j$ . Prove that:
\[ \sum_{i\equal{}1}^m\frac1{\binom{n\minus{}1}{|A_i|\minus{}1}}\leq1\]
solution_md:
By a *chain*, we denote a sequence of  $n$  subsets  $C_1, \cdots, C_n \subset [n]$  such that  $C_i\subset C_{i+1}$  for all  $1\le i < n$  and  $|C_i| = i$ . We double count pairs  $(A_i, C)$ , where  $C$  is a chain that contains  $A_i$ . On one hand, we have that for each  $A_i$ , there are  $(|A_i| !)(n - |A_i|)!$  chains that contain it. This gives  $$ \sum_i|A_i|!(n-|A_i|)! $$   pairs.

We say that a permutation  $\sigma$  of  $[n]$  *induces* a chain  $C$  if for all  $1\le i < n$ ,  $~C_{i+1} \setminus C_i = \{\sigma(i)\}$ . Say a chain  $C$  contains  $A_k$ . Let  $(c_1, c_2, ..., c_n)$  be the sequence that induces  $C$ . The key observation is that a chain induced by any sequence of the form  $(d_1, d_2, ... d_{n-|A_k|}, c_1, c_2, ..., c_{|A_k|})$  does not contain any element of  $A$ . If it contained  $A_i$ , then we would have that  $|A_i| + |A_k| > n$ , since  $|A_i|\cap |A_k| \neq \emptyset$ , which contradicts the problem statement. Therefore, any chain containing  $A_k$  also generates at least  $\big [ \frac{n}{2}\big ] !$  distinct chains not containing any  $A_i$ .

Now, any chain contains at most one  $A_i$ . Associated with each such chain is a unique set of at least  $\big [ \frac{n}{2}\big ] !$  chains not containing any  $A_j$ . There are a total of  $n!$  chains.Therefore, there are at most  $n! / \big [ \frac{n}{2}\big ] !$  pairs. This is at most  $(n-1)!$  for  $n \ge 6$ . In this case, we have that  $$ (n-1)! \ge \sum_i|A_i|!(n-|A_i|)! > \sum_i(|A_i|-1)!(n-|A_i|)!  $$  Dividing by  $(n-1)!$  gives the desired inequality. it remains to prove this when  $n < 6$ , which is easily done by exhaustion of cases.

Let  $ G=(V,E)$  be a simple graph.

a) Let  $ A,B$  be a subsets of  $ E$ , and spanning subgraphs of  $ G$  with edges  $ A,B,A\cup B$  and  $ A\cap B$  have  $ a,b,c$  and  $ d$  connected components respectively. Prove that  $ a+b\leq c+d$ .

We say that subsets  $ A_1,A_2,\dots,A_m$  of  $ E$  have  $ (R)$  property if and only if for each  $ I\subset\{1,2,\dots,m\}$  the spanning subgraph of  $ G$  with edges  $ \cup_{i\in I}A_i$  has at most  $ n-|I|$  connected components.
b) Prove that when  $ A_1,\dots,A_m,B$  have  $ (R)$  property, and  $ |B|\geq2$ , there exists an  $ x\in B$  such that  $ A_1,A_2,\dots,A_m,B\backslash\{x\}$  also have property  $ (R)$ .

Suppose that edges of  $ G$  are colored arbitrarily. A spanning subtree in  $ G$  is called colorful if and only if it does not have any two edges with the same color.
c) Prove that  $ G$  has a colorful subtree if and only if for each partition of  $ V$  to  $ k$  non-empty subsets such as  $ V_1,\dots,V_k$ , there are at least  $ k\minus{}1$  edges with distinct colors that each of these edges has its two ends in two different  $ V_i$ s.
d) Assume that edges of  $ K_n$  has been colored such that each color is repeated  $ \left[\frac n2\right]$  times. Prove that there exists a colorful subtree.
e) Prove that in part d) if  $ n\geq5$  there is a colorful subtree that is non-isomorphic to  $ K_{1,n-1}$ .
f) Prove that in part e) there are at least two non-intersecting colorful subtrees.
solution_md:
**b)** **Equivalent Problem:** Let  $G(V,E)$  be a graph such that  $|V|=n$  and  $E = A_1\cup A_2 \cup ... \cup A_m$ , where each  $A_j$  is non-empty and  $m\le n-1$ .  If  $G(V,E)$  has property  $(R)$  then there exists a subforest (collection of disjoint trees) whose edge set contains exactly one edge from each of the sets  $A_j$ .

*Note: you can observe that his problem is equivalent by repeatedly applying the original statement.*

*Proof:* Induction on  $m$ . If  $m=1$  then the statement is clearly true because  $A_1$  is not empty. Assume true for the case  $m-1$ .

If the set  $E_m = \{A_1,A_2...,A_m\}$  has property (R) then so does the set  $E_{m-1}=\{A_1,A_2...,A_{m-1}\}$ . By induction we can find a colourful subforest of  $G(V,E_{m-1})$ , call it  $T_0$ . If there exists an edge in  $A_m$  such that adding it to  $T_0$  will decrease the number of components of  $T_0$  then we're done. So assume the contrary.

By property (R) there must be an edge in a set  $A_j$  ( $j<m$ ) whose addition to  $T_0$  will decrease the number of components. Call all such edges *nice edges*, and call sets containing a nice edge, *nice sets*

Adding an edge from  $A_m$  to  $T_0$  will create a cycle in  $T_0$ . We can then remove any edge in this cycle to form a new subforest  $T_1$ . We call this process a *switch*; note that all edges of  $T$  have distinct colour after a switch and the set of *nice edges/nice sets* has not changed (*). So we wish to find a series of switches that ends in removing an edge from a nice set, because then we can add the nice edge from that set and decrease the number of components- giving us a forest with  $m$  edges.

We define the family of sets  $\mathcal{E}$ . If there is a series of *switches* that starts by adding edge  $x\in A_m$  to  $T_0$  and edges by removing edge  $y\in A_i$ , then place  $A_i \in \mathcal{E}$ . Also let  $A_m\in\mathcal{E}$ .

If  $\mathcal{E}$  contains a *nice set*,  $A_i$ , then by performing that series of switches we can remove and edge  $x\in A_i$  from that set and add the corresponding *nice edge*,  $y\in A_i$ . By the invariance property (*), this edge  $y$  will decreases the number of components of  $T$  - giving us a forest with  $m$  edges. 

If none of the sets in  $\mathcal{E}$  are nice then delete all edges from  $T_0$  that do not belong to a set in  $\mathcal{E}$ , call the new forest  $T^*$ .  $T^*$  has  $n-|\mathcal{E}|+1$  components (because  $A_m\in\mathcal{E}$ , but no edge from  $A_m\in E(T_0)$ ). Adding any edge  $x\in \mathcal{E}$  to  $T^*$  will not decrease the number of components, otherwise  $x$  would lie in a cycle of  $T_0$  with an edge  $y\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , contradicting the definition of  $\mathcal{E}$ . So in fact the graph with edge set  $\mathcal{E}$  also has  $n-|\mathcal{E}|+1$  components. But this contradicts property (R). 

This completes the inductive step  $\square$

**c)** Suppose the graph has the given property, call it property (P). Let  $A_1, A_2, ..., A_m$  be the edge sets of distinct colour in  $G$ . By applying property (P) for  $k=n$  it is clear that  $m\ge n-1$ . Further it is clear that the graph  $G$  is connected, for if we could partition  $G$  into two disconnected sets  $V_1$  and  $V_2$  with no edge between them, we would contradict property (P) for  $n=2$ .

Let  $F\subseteq G$  be the *largest* colourful forest, and let  $\mathcal{A}=\{A_1,A_2,...,A_j\}$  be the edge sets who have an edge in the forest. Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $j < n-1$ .

None of the remaining sets  $\{A_{j+1},...,A_m\}$  contains an edge that decreases the number of components of  $F$ . Therefore, such edge must exist in the set  $\mathcal{A}$  because  $G$  is connected. Let  $\mathcal{A}_1\subseteq \mathcal{A}$  be the sets that contain an edge,  $x$ , such that adding  $x$  to  $F$  will decrease the number of components

For  $k > j$ , adding an edge  $x \in A_k$  to  $F$  will create a cycle. You can then remove any edge from that cycle and you have a new colourful forest, call this operation a *switch* (as we did in part b).  If it was possible to remove an edge from a set  $A_i\in \mathcal{A}_1$  by a series of switches, then you could add the edge in  $y\in A_i$  to  $F$  and decrease the number of components (again like part b). This contradicts the fact that  $F$  is maximum. 

So it turns out that the graph with edges in the set  $\{A_1,....,A_m\} \backslash \mathcal{A}_1$  has at least  $n-j+\mathcal{A}_1$  components. By placing each of these components in its own set  $V_i$  and applying property (P) there are at least  $n-j+\mathcal{A}_1 -1$  other edges of distinct colour. These must come from the only remaining sets  $\mathcal{A}_1$ . But  $n-1-j+\mathcal{A}_1 > \mathcal{A}_1$  by assumption. This is a contradiction. 

Therefore  $F$  has at least  $n-1$  edges, that is, it has exactly  $n-1$ . So  $F\subset G$  is a colourful subtree.
 
This completes the proof of the *if* direction. The *only if* direction is more or less trivial, so the proof is complete  $\square$

**e)** *n is odd:* If there was a colourful subtree isomorphic to  $K_{1,n-1}$ , then we may remove the vertex of degree  $n-1$  and reduce the problem to the case of  $n-1$  vertices. If we find a desired subtree in the reduced graph then we add back the vertex we removed and connect it to the tree via the remaining edge of distinct colour. 

*n is even* Again, if there is a colourful subtree isomorphic to  $K_{1,n-1}$  we remove the root vertex. But this time we haven't reduced the problem entirely; there are too many colours. So pick an arbitrary colour, say blue, and re-colour the blue edges with the remaining colours (each remaining colour used on one blue edge). Then the problem has been reduced to the  $n-1$  vertices case.

In this manner we are done by induction if we can show the claim is true for  $n=5$ , but this is easily verified by hand. So the proof is complete  $\square$

**f)** We know that there exists at least one colourful subtree, so find one and remove those edges from the graph. Now each colour is repeated at most  $\frac{n-1}{2}$  times, and there are  $n-1$  pairs of vertices with no edges.

Therefore, as in part d, we require that  $\textstyle\sum_{i<j} v_iv_j \ge (k-2)\frac{n-1}{2} + 1 + (n-1)$ , where the  $n-1$  is accounting for the edges we removed. But we already showed in part d that the LHS is at least  $(n-1)(2n-k)$  so it's left to show that
\[(n-1)(2n-k) \ge (k-2)\frac{n-1}{2} + n\]
Which after some rearrangement becomes
\[nk \ge (k-1)^2 + 1\]
This is clearly true so the proof is complete  $\square$

solution_md:
a) This polynomial is reducible, as every polynomial of degree  $>2$  is reducible over  $\mathbb{R}$ .
b) This polynomial is irreducible. We can see immediately that it has no rational root.
Assume that  $t^{4}+1=(t^{2}+at+b)(t^{2}+ct+d)$ . Then we must have  $d=\frac{1}{b}, c=-a$ .
The remaining equations are  $a(\frac{1}{b}-b)=0$  and  $-a^{2}+b+\frac{1}{b}=0$ .
Since  $a=0$  is not possible due to the second equation, we get  $b=\pm 1$  and so  $a$  cannot be rational.
Therefore the polynomial is irreducible over  $\mathbb{Q}$ .
c) This polynomial is reducible, as  $t=1$  is a root.
d) This polynomial is irreducible. We can check that it has no root in  $\mathbb{Z}\slash 17\mathbb{Z}$ .
Assume that  $t^{4}+7=(t^{2}+at+b)(t^{2}+ct+d)$ . We get  $c=-a$ ,  $-a^{2}+b+d=0$  and  $a(d-b)=0$ .
If  $a=0$ , we obtain  $b=-d$ . This is not possible, as the equation  $-b^{2}=7$  has no solution.
If  $b=d$ , we obtain  $b^{2}=7$ . This equation has no solution either. Hence the polynomial is irreducible.
e) This polynomial is reducible, as  $t=3$  is a root.
f) This polynomial is irreducible. Observe that  $\mathbb{Z}[i]$  is a factorial ring, and since  $7\equiv 3$  (mod  $4$ ),  $7$  is a prime element in this ring.
Thus, by Eisenstein we conclude that this polynomial is irreducible in  $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ .

c) By giving an example show that if  $gcd([F(\alpha): F],[F(\beta): F])\neq 1$  then equality might happen.

**b)** Well, the whole extension  $K|F$  must contain sub-extensions of both coprime degrees, thus is a multiple of them, thus yes.

stem_md: If  $d\in \mathbb{Q}$ , is there always an  $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$  such that  $\omega ^n=1$  for some  $n\in \mathbb{N}$  and  $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})\subseteq \mathbb{Q}(\omega)$ ?
solution_md:
Yes, this is a special case of the Kronecker-Weber-Theorem that states that every finite abelian extension of  $\mathbb{Q}$  is contained in a cyclotomic extension.

For this case the gaussian sums  $\left(\sum_{n=1}^p \zeta^{n^2}\right)^2 = \pm p$  ( $p$  being prime,  $\zeta$  being a  $p$ -th root of unity) suffice to show that there is an extension containing  $\sqrt{p}$ , thus there is an extension containing  $\sqrt n$  for any integer  $n$ , and the result for rationals gets trivial.

stem_md: Suppose that  $X$  is a compact metric space and  $T: X\rightarrow X$  is a continous function. Prove that  $T$  has a returning point. It means there is a strictly increasing sequence  $n_i$  such that  $\lim_{k\rightarrow \infty} T^{n_k}(x_0)=x_0$  for some  $x_0$ .
solution_md:
I found this to be a pretty neat approach :).

Consider the locally convex vector space of real regular Borel measures on  $X$ , as the space of real functionals on  $C(X)$ , with the corresponding weak- $*$  topology. The set of probability measures on  $X$  is a convex compact set, on which  $T$  acts as a continuous map via  $T\mu(A)=\mu(T^{-1}(A))$  for all Borel subsets  $A$  of  $X$ . By standard fixed point theory, there is a probability measure  $\mu$  on  $X$  fixed by  $T$ , i.e. such that  $T$  is measure-preserving with respect to  $\mu$ . 

By the so-called Recurrence Theorem, for every Borel subset  $A$  of  $X$ , the set  $S_{A}$  of those  $x\in A$  for which only finitely many of the points  $T^{n}(x),\ n\ge 1$  belong to  $A$  has measure zero. 

Now let  $(U_{n})_{n}$  be a countable basis of open sets for  $X$ .  $S=\bigcup S_{U_{n}}$  then has measure zero, being a countable union of sets of measure zero, so every point  $x$  of  $X\setminus S$  has the property that whenever  $x\in U$  ( $U$  being an open subset of  $X$ ), infinitely many of the points  $T^{n}(x)$  belong to  $U$ . The conclusion follows, since any such  $x$  is a returning point.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Iran Contests/Pre-Preparation Course Examination/2006 Pre-Preparation Course Examination/75825.json

candidates:
I remembered this while working on something similar. Here's a shorter proof:

Consider the collection of all closed subsets of  $ X$  invariant under  $ T$  (i.e. mapped into themselves by  $ T$ ). By Zorn's Lemma, a member  $ F$  of this collection which is minimal with respect to inclusion can be found. It follows from minimality that for every  $ x\in F$ , the orbit  $ \{T^{n}x\ |\ n\ge 0\}$  of  $ x$  is dense in  $ F$ , and hence every point of  $ F$  is a returning point.

stem_md:
Show that if  $f: [0,1]\rightarrow [0,1]$  is a continous function and it has topological transitivity then periodic points of  $f$  are dense in  $[0,1]$ .
Topological transitivity means there for every open sets  $U$  and  $V$  there is  $n>0$  such that  $f^n(U)\cap V\neq \emptyset$ .
solution_md:
Suppose we can find a non-degenerate compact subinterval  $ I$  of  $ [0,1]$  in which  $ f$  has no periodic points. I'll denote the  $ n$ 'th iterate of  $ f$  by  $ f^{n}$ , and the identity map on some subset  $ A$  of  $ [0,1]$  by  $ 1_{A}$ . Notice that  $ f^{n}(I),\ n\ge 0$  are all compact intervals (possibly degenerate). We want to reach a contradiction; we do this in a series of steps:


(1) *None of the intervals  $ f^{n}(I)$  contains a fixed point of  $ f$*

Let  $ y\in f^{n}(I)$  be a fixed point of  $ f$ , for some  $ n\ge 0$ . Our assumption that  $ I$  contains no periodic points implies that for all  $ n\ge 1,\ f^{n}-1_{I}$  has constant sign. If  $ x\in I$  such that  $ f^{n}(x)=y$  (which is, by assumption, different from  $ x$ ), then  $ f^{m}(x)-x$  has the same sign for all  $ m\ge n$ , and in conclusion  $ f^{m}-1_{I}$  has the same sign for all  $ m\ge n$ . This is easily seen to contradict the topological transitivity of  $ f$ . 


(2) *None of the intervals  $ f^{n}(I)$  contains a periodic point of  $ f$*

Assume we can find a periodic point  $ y\in f^{n}(I)$  for some  $ n\ge 0$ , and let  $ T\ge 1$  be its period. Then, for all  $ m\ge n$ , the interval  $ f^{m}(I)$  intersects one of the intervals  $ f^{n}(I),\ \ldots,\ f^{n+T-1}(I)$ , and hence the number of connected components of the sets  $ S_{p}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{p}f^{i}(I),\ p\ge 0$  is bounded. Combined with the fact that, by transitivity,  $ \bigcup_{p}S_{p}$  is dense in  $ [0,1]$ , this implies that  $ [0,1]\setminus\bigcup_{p}S_{p}$  is a finite set  $ \{x_{i}\ |\ 1\le i\le k\}$  (intuitively speaking, because the number of components of  $ S_{p}$  is bounded, increasing  $ p$  only enlarges these finitely many intervals, and the points left out are the finitely many "caught between" the intervals). Of course, by (1), the fixed points of  $ f$  are among the  $ x_{i}$ . We actually prove that the  $ x_{i}$  are precisely the fixed points of  $ f$ . Assume, for instance, that  $ x_{1}<x_{3}$  are fixed points of  $ f$ , that  $ f>1_{(x_{1},x_{3})}$ , and that  $ x_{2}\in(x_{1},x_{3})$  is the smallest  $ x_{i}$  larger than  $ x_{1}$  (the other cases can be treated similarly). Then, because  $ f(x_{2})>x_{2},\ p$  can be chosen so large that  $ x_{2}\in S_{p}$  (a picture should clear things up), contradicting the definition of the set  $ \{x_{i}\}$ . We have thus shown that  $ \{x_{i}\}$  is the set of fixed points of  $ f$ . 

If  $ x_{1}<x_{2}$  are consecutive fixed points, then  $ \left(\bigcup S_{p}\right)\cap(x_{1},x_{2})=(x_{1},x_{2})$ , so  $ f$  cannot take the values  $ x_{1},x_{2}$  inside  $ (x_{1},x_{2})$ . This implies that  $ f$  maps  $ (x_{1},x_{2})$  into itself, and for all  $ x\in(x_{1},x_{2})$  the sequence  $ f^{n}(x),\ n\ge 0$  is strictly monotonic. Clearly, this contradicts the transitivity of  $ f$ . There is now only one case left, namely the case when  $ f$  has exactly one fixed point  $ x_{1}$ . It follows from our previous discussion that  $ f$  takes the value  $ x_{1}$  precisely in  $ x_{1}$ , and that  $ f-x_{1}$  has constant and opposite signs on the intervals  $ (0,x_{1})$  and  $ (x_{1},1)$ . If  $ f<x_{1}$  on  $ (0,x_{1})$ , then the resriction of  $ f$  to  $ [0,x_{1}]$  has topological trnsitivity, and also satisfies  $ f>1_{[0,x_{1}]}$ , two facts which are incompatible (I assume here that  $ x_{1}\not\in\{0,1\}$ ). On the other hand, if  $ f>x_{1}$  on  $ (0,x_{1})$  and  $ f^{2}$  has no fixed points in  $ [0,x_{1}]$  other than  $ x_{1}$ , then the previous sentence applies to  $ f^{2}$  (not that in this case  $ f^{2}$  does indeed have topological transitivity on  $ [0,x_{1}]$ ). Finally, if  $ f>x_{1}$  on  $ (0,x_{1})$  and  $ f^{2}$  has a fixed point in  $ [0,x_{1}]$  other than  $ x_{1}$ , then we can work with the restriction of  $ f^{2}$  to  $ [0,x_{1}]$  which now has at least two fixed points, a case which has already been treated. This finishes the proof of (2).


(3) *The end of the proof*

(2) says, basically, that for all  $ m\ne m,\ f^{m}-f^{n}$  is non-zero and hence has constant sign on  $ I$ . By transitivity, we can find  $ n$  such that  $ f^{n}(I)\cap I\ne\emptyset$  and  $ f^{n}>1_{I}$  (call these two conditions  $ (*)$ ), and we can find  $ m$  such that  $ f^{m}(I)\cap I\ne\emptyset$  and  $ f^{m}<1_{I}$  (similarly, denote these two conditions by  $ (**)$ ). Check now that  $ (*)$ , together with the previous observation, implies  $ f^{mn}>1_{I}$ , while  $ (**)$  implies  $ f^{mn}<1_{I}$ . This provides the contradiction we were looking for.

You have to find whether the density of those  $n$  for which  $\left\{n\log_{10}2\right\}\in(\log_{10}3,\log_{10}4)$  (the necessary and sufficient condition for  $2^n$  to begin with  $3$ ) is larger than that of those  $n$  for which  $\left\{\log_{10}2\right\}\in(\log_{10}4,\log_{10}5)$  (the necessary and sufficient condition for  $2^n$  to begin with  $4$ ). solution_md:
I know this is an old thread,but I'm looking for a solution for part **b)**,I thought asking it here is better than posting it again,so does anyone have a solution for part **b**? :maybe:
*Double Counting* : LHS can be interpreted in the following way : Choose $ k$ elements from a set $ M$ with $ |M|\equal{}n$ elements in $ \binom {m}{k}$ distinct ways. Consider another set $ N$ (with $ |N|\equal{}n$ elements) disjoint from $ M$ . Choose $ m$ elements from the union of the set $ N$ and $ k$ elements previously chosen. One can do this in $ \binom {n\plus{}k}{m}$ distinct ways. It follows that the number of ordered pairs of sets $ (X,Y)$ where $ X \subset M$ , $ Y \subset N \cup X$ with $ |X|\equal{}k$ , $ |Y|\equal{}m$ is equal to $ \binom {m}{k}\binom {n\plus{}k}{m}$ . If the result is extended to $ k$ which varies from $ 0$ to $ m$ , the number of all pairs $ (X,Y)$ will be equal to $ \sum_{k\equal{}0}^m \binom {m}{k} \binom {n\plus{}k}{m}$ . This problem can also be solved by first choosing the sets $ Y \cap M$ and $ Y \cap N$ . If $ |Y \cap N|\equal{}j$ , then $ 0 \leq j\leq m$ and it follows that $ |Y \cap M|\equal{}m\minus{}j$ . Thus we can choose $ Y$ so that $ |Y \cap N|\equal{}j$ and $ |Y \cap M|\equal{}m\minus{}j$ in $ \binom {n}{j}\binom {m}{m\minus{}j}$ different ways. It remains to choose the set $ X$ so as to satisfy $ Y \cap M \subset X \subset M$ , since $ Y \subset N \cup X$ and thus $ Y \cap M \subset (N \cup X) \cap M\equal{}(N \cap M) \cup (X \cap M)\equal{}\null \cup X\equal{}X$ . But the set $ X$ can be chosen in $ 2^j$ ways, because for each of the $ j$ elements of the set $ M\ (Y \cap M)$ there exist exactly two possibilities: it belongs or does not belong to the set $ X$ . It follows that the number of pairs $ (X,Y)$ with the stated property is equal to $ \sum_{j\equal{}0}^m \binom {n}{j} \binom {m}{j}2^j$ , and this observation completes the proof of **(b)**.

stem_md: Suppose that  $p(n)$  is the number of ways to express  $n$  as a sum of some naturall numbers (the two representations  $4=1+1+2$  and  $4=1+2+1$  are considered the same). Prove that for an infinite number of  $n$ 's  $p(n)$  is even and for an infinite number of  $n$ 's  $p(n)$  is odd.
solution_md:
Well, this one, **delegat**, is really well-known, and thus has surely been discussed before on ML.

That said, it's quickly proved with generating functions, so I'll write it here :
let  $ D$  be the number of ways in which  $ n$  can be expressed as a sum of different positive integers and let  $ O$  be the number of ways in which  $ n$  can be expressed as a sum of odd positive integers,
then  $ D = (1 + x)(1 + x^2)\cdots = \frac {1 - x^2^}{1 - x} \cdot \frac {1 - x^4}{1 - x^2^} \cdots = \frac 1{1 - x} \cdot \frac 1{1 - x^3^} \cdots = O.$ 
(of course, I can't help but recommend [generatingfunctionology](http://www.math.upenn.edu/~wilf/gfology2.pdf) by Herbert Wilf)

That said, there is a bijective proof of this fact, which I invite you to try and find.
For more of those, see also [# of partitions of type 1 = # of partitions of type 2](http://www.mathlinks.ro/viewtopic.php?t=26379)


Now, as for the original problem of this thread, it should be mentioned that the parity of  $ p(n)$  is in general a very difficult problem. (this question was raised by Ramanujan)
This particular problem was solved by Kolberg in the 60's, and his proof is based on the identities : $ \sum_{n \ge 0} p(n) x^n = \prod_{n \ge 1} \frac 1{1 - x^n}$ 
and $ \prod_{n \ge 1} (1 - x^n) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} ( - 1)^nx^{(3n^2 + n)/2}.$  (namely, the [Pentagonal Number Theorem](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/PentagonalNumberTheorem.html))

Actually, a pretty hard conjecture is that, (roughly,) the partition function takes as many even values as odd values.

stem_md: $D$  is an arbitrary point inside triangle  $ABC$ , and  $E$  is inside triangle  $BDC$ . Prove that \[\frac{S_{DBC}}{(P_{DBC})^{2}}\geq\frac{S_{EBC}}{(P_{EBC})^{2}}\]
solution_md:
Solution:
Let  $r_{1}$  be the inradius of  $\triangle{DBC}$  and  $r_{2}$  be the inradius of  $\triangle{EBC}$ . For convenience, denote $\angle{DBC},\angle{BCD},\angle{BDC}, \angle{EBC},\angle{BCE},\angle{BEC}$  as  $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}$ 
Then it's to prove $\frac{r_{1}}{P(DBC)}\geq \frac{r_{2}}{P(EBC)}$ 
Since $P(DBC)=2r_{1}(\cot{\frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}}+\cot{\frac{\alpha_{2}}{2}}+\cot{\frac{\alpha_{3}}{2}})$ 
and do the same thing for $P(EBC)$ 
Then we need to prove  $\cot{\frac{\beta_{1}}{2}}+\cot{\frac{\beta_{2}}{2}}+\cot{\frac{\beta_{3}}{2}}\geq cot{\frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}}+\cot{\frac{\alpha_{2}}{2}}+\cot{\frac{\alpha_{3}}{2}}$ 
since  $cot(x)$  is convex on $(0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$  and  $(\beta_{3};\beta_{2};\beta_{1})\succ (\alpha_{3};\alpha_{2};\alpha_{1})$ 
use Karamata and the proof is finished.

stem_md: $ABC$  is an arbitrary triangle.  $A',B',C'$  are midpoints of arcs  $BC, AC, AB$ . Sides of triangle  $ABC$ , intersect sides of triangle  $A'B'C'$  at points  $P,Q,R,S,T,F$ . Prove that \[\frac{S_{PQRSTF}}{S_{ABC}}=1-\frac{ab+ac+bc}{(a+b+c)^{2}}\]
solution_md: **Proof.** Denote $S\equiv [ABC]$ , $S_{h}\equiv [PQRSTF]$ , $S'\equiv [A'B'C']$ . Suppose $\{P,Q\}\subset BC$ , $\{R,S\}\subset CA$ , $\{T,F\}\subset AB$ . Prove easily that $AA'\perp B'C'$ . Thus, $\{\begin{array}{c}B'A=B'I\ ,\ IB\cdot IB'=2Rr\ \frac{TA}{TB}=\frac{B'A}{B'B}\end{array}$ $\Longrightarrow$ $\frac{TA}{IB'}=\frac{TB}{IB'+IB}=\frac{c}{2\cdot IB'+IB}$ $\Longrightarrow$ $TA=$ $\frac{c\cdot IB'}{2\cdot IB'+IB}=$ $\frac{c\cdot IB'\cdot IB}{2\cdot IB'\cdot IB+IB^{2}}=$ $\frac{c\cdot 2Rr}{4Rr+\frac{ac(p-b)}{p}}=$ $\frac{4Rrp\cdot c}{8Rrp+2ac(p-b)}=$ $\frac{abc\cdot c}{2abc+2ac(p-b)}=$ $\frac{bc}{2b+(a+c-b)}=$ $\frac{bc}{2p}\Longrightarrow$ $\boxed{TA=\frac{bc}{2p}}$ . Therefore, $S_{h}=S-\sum(\frac{bc}{2p})^{2}\sin A=S-\frac{S}{4p^{2}}\cdot\sum bc=S\cdot[1-\frac{ab+bc+ca}{(a+b+c)^{2}}]$ . $ab+bc+ca=p^{2}+r^{2}+4Rr\Longrightarrow$ $\boxed{S_{h}=\frac{r}{4p}\cdot(3p^{2}-r^{2}-4Rr)}$ .**Remarks.** $1.\blacktriangleright\{\begin{array}{c}3(ab+bc+ca)\le (a+b+c)^{2}\Longrightarrow \boxed{S_{h}\ge \frac{2}{3}\cdot S}\ S'=2R^{2}\cos\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{B}{2}\cos\frac{C}{2}=\frac{pR}{2}\Longrightarrow \boxed{S'=\frac{pR}{2}}\ge pr=S\Longrightarrow \boxed{S'\ge S}\end{array}$ . $2.\blacktriangleright\sqrt 3\le\frac{4R+r}{p}\le\frac{p}{3r}$ $\Longrightarrow$ $S_{h}=\frac{r}{4p}\cdot[3p^{2}-r(4R+r)]\le$ $\frac{r}{4p}\cdot [(4R+r)^{2}-r(4R+r)]=$ $\frac{Rr(4R+r)}{p}\le$ $\frac{Rp}{3}=$ $\frac{2}{3}\cdot S'$ $\Longrightarrow$ $\boxed{S_{h}\le\frac{2}{3}\cdot S'}$ . In conclusion, $\boxed{\frac{2}{3}\cdot S\le S_{h}\le\frac{2}{3}\cdot S'}$ .

stem_md: Let  $a\geq 2$  be a natural number. Prove that  $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac1{a^{n^{2}}}$  is irrational.
solution_md:
Actually, I didn't have Roth's theorem in mind when I said that it's not too difficult to prove the transcendence of  $\sum a^{-2^{n}}$ ; and I will give a self-contained proof in the next post. But first, let's see how Roth actually DOES imply this fact pretty easily :). Well, maybe not the most classical version of Roth, but rather two [I will give proofs by] two different strengthenings of it. 

The first more general Roth result (due to Schmidt, and the very special case of his "subspace theorem") is as follows: for any algebraic numbers  $\alpha_{0}, \ldots, \alpha_{d}\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$  and every  $\varepsilon > 0$ , the inequality  $0 < |\alpha_{0}x_{0}+\cdots+\alpha_{d}x_{d}| < \max_{i}\{|x_{i}|\}^{-d-\varepsilon}$  has only finitely many solutions in integers  $x_{0}, \ldots,x_{d}$ ; this is basically the most basic version of Roth's result in dimension  $d$ , with the classical Roth result appearing as  $d=1$ . To deduce from the theorem just stated the transcendence of  $\sum a^{-2^{n}}$ , we will only use the case  $d=2$  and  $\alpha_{0}: = 1, \alpha_{1}: = \beta, \alpha_{2}: = \beta^{2}$ , where  $\beta : = \sum a^{-2^{n}}$ . Letting  $\beta_{n}: = \sum_{k \leq n}a^{-2^{k}}$ , the rational approximation  $|\beta-\beta_{n}| = a^{-2^{n+1}}+a^{-2^{n+2}}+\cdots = O(a^{-2^{n+1}})$  is good, but not good enough to apply Roth to it directly. Instead, one looks at an identity like
 $(\beta-\beta_{n})^{2}-2a^{-2^{n+1}}(\beta-\beta_{n})+a^{-2^{n+1}}-(\beta-\beta_{n}) = (a^{-2^{n+1}}+\cdots)^{2}-2a^{-2^{n+1}}(a^{-2^{n+1}}+\cdots)+a^{-2^{n+1}}-(a^{-2^{n+1}}+\cdots) =-a^{-6 \cdot 2^{n+1}}+\cdots = O(a^{-6 \cdot 2^{n+1}}),$ 

and sees that it is good enough to imply the desired transcendence: one applies the above-mentioned result with, say,  $\varepsilon = 1/2$  (any  $\varepsilon < 1$  will do).


An alternative way to "see" the transcendence of  $\sum a^{-2^{n}}$  is by another, this time much more straightforward, generalization of Roth: by approximating directly, but using several absolute values at once. Such result was first given by Ridout (and, afterwards, Mahler), and the simplest version reads: 
**Roth's theorem with several absolute values.** Let  $S$  be a finite set of primes, including the "infinite prime," the symbol  $\infty$ . For every  $p \in S$  we have the  $p$ -adic absolute value  $|\cdot|_{p}$  on  $\mathbb{Q}$ , normalized as usual: if  $p = \infty$ , then  $|\cdot|$  is the "standard" archimedean absolute value; if  $p$  is finite, then  $|x|_{p}: = p^{-\mathrm{ord}_{p}{x}}$ .

For every  $p \in S$ , consider an algebraic number  $\alpha_{p}\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Extend each absolute value  $|\cdot|_{p}$  to  $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_{p})$  in some way. Then for every  $\varepsilon > 0$  there are only finitely many rational solutions  $r/s$  to the inequality
\[\prod_{p \in S}|\alpha_{p}-r/s|_{p}< s^{-2-\varepsilon}. \]
To deduce the transcendence of  $\beta = \sum a^{-2^{n}}$ , take  $S$  to consist of  $\infty$  and the finitely many prime divisors of  $a$ . Choose  $\alpha_{\infty}: = 1/\beta$ , and for the other  $p$ s, choose  $\alpha_{p}: = 0$ . Of course, we then choose  $r/s : = 1/\beta_{n}= \big( \sum_{k \leq n}a^{-2^{k}}\big)^{-1}$ , with  $r = a^{2^{n}}$  (this time we approximate directly). Then  $|\alpha_{\infty}-r/s|_{\infty}= |1/\beta-1/\beta_{n}| = |\beta-\beta_{n}| / |\beta\beta_{n}| < 2 a^{-2^{n+1}}$  and  $\prod_{p \in S \setminus \{ \infty\}}|\alpha_{p}-r/s|_{p}= \prod_{p \mid a}|r/s|_{p}= \prod_{p \mid a}|a^{2^{n}}|_{p}= a^{-2^{n}}$ , whence  $\prod_{p \in S}|\alpha_{p}-r/s|_{p}< 2a^{-3 \cdot 2^{n}}$ , and this is true for every  $n$ , contradicting the above-stated inequality for any  $\varepsilon < 1$ .


Now, I had the intention to write a self-contained (and not too long) proof of the transcendence of  $\sum a^{-2^{n}}$  in my next post, but now that I explained how to deduce this from the two-dimensional Roth theorem, I see that what I wrote there is an excellent hint on how to proceed "ad hoc," without recourse to Roth. This hint should really convey the essential point in the proof; if it doesn't, then I'll write the proof myself. 

Finally, notice that the second deduction from "Roth-type" generalizes immediately to show: if  $n_{0}< n_{1}< \cdots$  is an increasing sequence with  $\lim\sup n_{i+1}/n_{i}> 3/2$ , then  $\sum a^{-n_{i}}$  is transcendental. (The "classical" Roth theorem immediately told us that this were the case if the weaker condition  $\lim\sup n_{i+1}/n_{i}> 2$ , which did not suffice for the problem, held). A similar argument, slightly refined, would show that it suffices to assume  $\lim\sup n_{i+1}/n_{i}> 1$ ; in particular,  taking on Rust's example,  $\sum a^{-\lfloor b^{n}\rfloor}$  is transcendental for any integer  $a > 1$  and any real  $b > 1$ . Further, along similar lines (but we'd have to recourse to Schmidt's far-reaching generalization of Roth -- the one-dimensional case won't suffice anymore, even in the case that  $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ !), it is possible to show that  $\sum \alpha^{n_{i}}$  is transcendental for any  $\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$  algebraic with  $|\alpha| < 1$ , and  $n_{0}< n_{1}< \cdots$  with  $\lim\sup n_{i+1}/n_{i}> 1$ !


Now, I leave you the pleasure of proving the transcendence of  $\sum a^{-2^{n}}$  without recourse to Roth's theorem :) The hint is very explicit in the first part of this post. On the other hand, for the stronger problems with the  $n_{i}$ , I don't think think it would be possible to give a short proof avoiding Roth or a result of comparable depth (the approach I know for  $\sum a^{-2^{n}}$  certainly breaks down if we try this more general problem... )

stem_md:
This question is both combinatorics and Number Theory :
a ) Prove that we can color edges of  $K_{p}$  with  $p$  colors which is proper, ( $p$  is an odd prime) and  $K_{p}$  can be partitioned to  $\frac{p-1}2$  rainbow Hamiltonian cycles. (A Hamiltonian cycle is a cycle that passes from all of verteces, and a rainbow is a subgraph that all of its edges have different colors.)
b) Find all answers of  $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1$  is  $\mathbb Z_{p}$
solution_md:
Here is my solution to (a):
Numbering vertex  $0, 1, ...$  to  $p-1$  and consider the graph as the  $\mathbb Z_{p}$  aditive cyclic group. Since  $p$  is and odd prime and the graph is complete, we have  $\frac{p(p-1)}2$  edges. Denote by  $i--j$  the edge joining vertex  $i$  and  $j$ .
Notice that being  $\mathbb Z_{p}$  cyclic, we have a cycle of vertex iff we make a "generator" route, i.e., making  $0--k--2k--...--(p-1)k--0$  cycle where k is a generator.
There are  $p-1$  generators in  $\mathbb Z_{p}$ , so we have exactly  $\frac{p-1}2$  of these cycles (notice that cycle  $0--i--2i--...$  is the same to cycle  $0--(p-i)--2(p-i)--...$  in backward sense). Each of these cycles pass once in each of the vertex, and has exactly  $p$  edges, no one ocurring in another cycle. Therefore, we have partitioned the graph in  $\frac{p-1}2$  Hamiltonian cycles. Coloring each edge with one of the  $p$  colors in each of the subgraphs, we obtain the required rainbow partition.

stem_md:
a) There is an infinite sequence of  $0,1$ , like  $\dots,a_{-1},a_{0},a_{1},\dots$  (i.e. an element of  $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ ). At each step we make a new sequence. There is a function  $f$  such that for each  $i$ ,  $\mbox{new }a_{i}=f(a_{i-100},a_{i-99},\dots,a_{i+100})$ . This operation is mapping  $F: \{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ . Prove that if  $F$  is 1-1, then it is surjective.
b) Is the statement correct if we have an  $f_{i}$  for each  $i$ ?
solution_md:
Part a):

Let's take a finite string of 0,1 s.
It's well-known that the probability that a long string hasn't got s as a substring tends to 0.
If we consider the image of the set S formed by all infinite strings having  $ a_i=0$  if  $ i \le 0$  or  $ i > N$ . f is injective, so  $ f(S)$  has  $ 2^{N}$  elements. If we cut the strings of  $ f(S)$  from character  $ -99$  to character  $ N+100$ , we must find again  $ 2^{N}$  different strings of length  $ N+200$ . So, the probability that we can find a given string of length k in the image is at least  $ 2^{-200}$ .

Therefore, s must be in the image  $ \Rightarrow$  we can find all finite strings in the image of f.

Now the cool part:  $ \{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ , with product topology, as product of compact hausdorff spaces, is compact hausdorff itself. f is continuous in this topology (since if two strings are equal in a "big enough" part, so are their images), therefore the image is closed. But the image contains all finite strings, and we can also translate them, so the image is dense. QED  :D

\[a^2-ab+b^2|(ab)^2\]
solution_md:

Let  $1 \leq m = \min S$  and  $a \in S$ . Also let  $d = \gcd(m,a)$  and so  $m = dx$ ,  $b = dy$ , with  $\gcd(x,y) = 1$ .
Then we need  $x^2 - xy + y^2 \mid d^2x^2y^2$ ; but  $\gcd(x^2 - xy + y^2,x) = \gcd(x^2 - xy + y^2,y) = 1$ , so we need  $x^2 - xy + y^2 \mid d^2$ , therefore  $1 \leq x^2 - xy + y^2 \leq d^2$  (since  $x^2 - xy + y^2 = (x-y/2)^2 + 3(y/2)^2 > 0$ ).

Then  $m^2 - ma + a^2 = d^2(x^2 - xy + y^2) \leq d^4 \leq m^4$ , so  $a^2 - ma + m^2 - m^4 \leq 0$ , but the number of such positive integers  $a$  is finite, so  $S$  must be finite.

Notice that there exist such finite sets  $S$ , as numerous as we want. Take  $S = \{kd \ ; \ 1 \leq k \leq n\}$ , with  $|S| = n$ ; it is enough to impose  $p^2 - pq + q^2 \mid d^2$  for all  $1\leq p, q \leq n$ , and we can take  $d = \prod_{1\leq p, q \leq n} (p^2 - pq + q^2)$ .

stem_md: Prove that  $2^{2^{n}}+2^{2^{{n-1}}}+1$  has at least  $n$  distinct prime divisors.
solution_md:
We will proceed with induction.
Base Case:  $n=0,1,2$ It works of course!
Inductive Step: Assume it works till  $k=n-1$  and proof for  $k = n$ .
Let  $x = 2^{2^{n-2}}$ .
Thus  $2^{2^{n}}+2^{2^{{n-1}}}+1 = x^4 + x^2 + 1 = \left(x^2 + x + 1\right)\left(x^2 - x + 1\right) = \left(2^{2^{n-1}} + 2^{2^{n-2}} + 1\right)\left(x^2 -x + 1\right)$ .
By induction,  $2^{2^{n-1}} + 2^{2^{n-2}} + 1$  has at least  $n-1$  distinct prime divisors. $\gcd(x^2 + x  +1, x^2 - x + 1) = \gcd(x^2 + x + 1 , 2x) = \gcd(x^2  + x + 1,x) = 1$ .
Thus, for  $x > 1$   $\exists$  a prime  $p$  such that  $p \nmid x^2 + x + 1$  but  $p \mid x^4 + x^2 + 1$ .
Hence  $\exists$   $n$  distinct prime divisors of  $2^{2^{n}}+2^{2^{{n-1}}}+1$  by induction.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
For a positive integer  $n$ , denote  $rad(n)$  as product of prime divisors of  $n$ . And also  $rad(1)=1$ . Define the sequence  $\{a_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$  in this way:  $a_1 \in \mathbb N$  and for every  $n \in \mathbb N$ ,  $a_{n+1}=a_n+rad(a_n)$ . 
Prove that for every  $N \in \mathbb N$ , there exist  $N$  consecutive terms of this sequence which are in an arithmetic progression.
solution_md: Observe that    $a_{k+1}=a_k+rad(a_k)\leq 2a_k$  for all  $k$  so that   $a_n\leq 2^{n-1}a_1$  for all  $n$ . On the other hand,   $a_{k+1}=a_k+rad(a_k)$  is divisible by  $rad(a_k)$ , hence  $rad(a_{k+1})$  is divisible by  $rad(a_k)$  for all  $k$ .   Assume to the contrary that for some positive integer  $N$  there are no consecutive  $N$  terms of this sequence forming an arithmetic progression.  This exactly means that there are no consecutive  $N-1$  terms, having the same radical. In other words, if we write down all the terms of this sequence then we will notice that after every  $N-1$  steps we get a new prime factor in the prime factorization of the  considered term.  This means that    $a_n$  has at least  $\lfloor n/(N-1) \rfloor$  prime factors and therefore is greater than  $ (\lfloor n/(N-1) \rfloor)!$  for all  $n$ .  In the long run we  get that  $2^na_1\geq a_n>(\lfloor n/(N-1) \rfloor)!$  for all  $n$ , which is a contradiction, since the latter inequality is valid only for finite number of values of  $n$ . The attained contradiction proves the statement.

Find all functions  $f : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N$  such that:

i)  $f^{2000}(m)=f(m)$  for all  $m \in \mathbb N$ ,

ii)  $f(mn)=\dfrac{f(m)f(n)}{f(\gcd(m,n))}$ , for all  $m,n\in \mathbb N$ , and

iii)  $f(m)=1$  if and only if  $m=1$ .
solution_md:
$f$ is multiplicative.
PROOFWhen $m$ and $n$ are coprime $gcd(m , n)=1$ so by condition 2 and 3: $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$
$f(m^n)=f(m), \forall m,n\in\mathbb{N}$
PROOFBase Case: $m=1$ (trivial) Inductive Step: Assume that $f(m^k)=f(m)$ where $k\in\mathbb{N}$ $n=m^k$ in condition 2: $f(m^{k+1})=\frac{f(m^k)f(m)}{f(m)}=f(m^k)=f(m)$ This completes the inductive step so, by induction, $f(m^n)=f(m), \forall m,n\in\mathbb{N}$
LEMMA 1: $f\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}^{a_i}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}f(p_i)$ where $a_i\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p_i$ is a different prime number for each $i\in\{1, \cdots , k\}$
PROOF$f$ is multiplicative so $f\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}^{a_i}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}f(p_i^{a_i})$ where $a_i\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p_i$ is a different prime number for each $i\in\{1, \cdots , k\}$ But $f(m^n)=f(m), \forall m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ so $\prod_{i=1}^{k}f(p_i^{a_i})=\prod_{i=1}^{k}f(p_i)$ So $f\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}^{a_i}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}f(p_i)$ where $a_i\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p_i$ is a different prime number for each $i\in\{1, \cdots , k\}$
LEMMA 2: Suppose that $f(x)=f(p)$ where $p$ is a prime number, then $x$ is a power of $p$ .
PROOFIf $q|x$ and $q$ is a prime number not equal to $p$ . Then by LEMMA 1: $f(q)|f(x)$ so $f(q)|f(p)$ $f(q)|f(p)\implies gcd(f(p),f(q))=f(q)$ $m=f(p)$ and $n=f(q)$ in condition two: $f(f(p)f(q))=\frac{f(f(p))f(f(q))}{f(f(q))}=f(f(p))$ $f$ is multiplicative (and after applying condition 1 twice), we get $f(p)f(q)=f(pq)=f^{2000}(pq)=f^{1999}(f(p)f(q))=f^{2000}(p)=f(p)$ $f(p)f(q)=f(p)\implies f(q)=1\implies q=1$ by condition 3, CONTRADICTION. So if $q|x$ and $q$ is a prime then $q=p$ Hence if $f(x)=f(p)$ where $p$ is a prime number, then $x$ is a power of $p$ .
Now $f(f^{1999}(p))=f(p)$ so by LEMMA 2, $f^{1999}(p)$ is a power of $p$ . LEMMA 3: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a power of a prime then so is $x$ .
PROOFLet $f(x)=p^a$ and $x=\prod_{i=1}^{k}q_{i}^{a_{i}}$ where $\forall i\in\{1, \cdots, k\}$ , $q_i$ is a prime number and $a_i\in\mathbb{N}$ By LEMMA 1, we get $\prod_{i=1}^{k}f(q_i)=f(x)=p^a$ So $f(q_i)$ is a power of $p$ , $\forall i\in\{1, \cdots, k\}$ Let $f(q_i)=p^{b_i}$ , where $b_i\in\mathbb{N}$ $\forall i\in\{1, \cdots, k\}$ If $k>1$ , then $f(q_1)$ and $f(q_2)$ are power of $p$ $b_1\leq b_2$ or $b_2\leq b_1$ so $f(q_1)|f(q_2)$ or $f(q_2)|f(q_1)$ . W.L.O.G. we can assume that $f(q_1)|f(q_2)$ so $gcd(f(q_1), f(q_2))=f(q_1)$ $m=f(q_1)$ and $n=f(q_2)$ in condition two: $f(f(q_1)f(q_2))=\frac{f(f(q_1))f(f(q_2))}{f(f(q_1))}=f(f(q_2))$ $f$ is multiplicative (and after applying condition 1 twice), we get $f(q_1)f(q_2)=f(q_1q_2)=f^{2000}(q_1q_2)=f^{1999}(f(q_1)f(q_2))=f^{2000}(q_2)=f(q_2)$ $f(q_1)f(q_2)=f(q_2)\implies f(q_1)=1\implies q_1=1$ CONTRADICTION. So $k=1\implies x$ is a power of a prime. So if $f(x)$ is a power of a prime then so is $x$
By applying LEMMA 3 on $f^{1999}(p)$ which is a power of a prime, (1998 times) we get that $f(p)$ is a power of a prime $\forall $ prime numbers $p$ Denote the $i^{th}$ prime number by $p_i$ So there must exist functions $G$ and $I$ such that $f(p_{i})=p_{G(i)}^{I(p_i)}$ because $f(p)$ is a power of a prime $\forall $ prime numbers $p$ (the prime number is dependant on $p$ which is dependant on $i$ where $p$ is the $i^{th}$ prime number, and the power of the prime is dependant on the the prime $p$ ) $f(m^n)=f(m)$ where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers but if $n=0$ then $f(m^n)=f(1)$ If we now define the function $H$ which maps $0$ to $0$ and the natural numbers to $1$ $f(m^n)=f(m^{H(n)})$ Then $f(p_{i}^{a_i})=p_{G(i)}^{H(a_i)I(p_i)}$ By LEMMA 1, we get $f\left(\prod_{i=1}p_{i}^{a_i}\right)=\prod_{i=1}p_{G(i)}^{H(a_i)I(p_i)}$ Also $f^{1999}(p_i)=p_{G^{1999}(i)}^{I(p_{G^{1999}(i)})}$ is a power of $p_i, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}$ So $G^{1999}(i)=i, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}$ $1999$ is a prime number so split $\mathbb{N}$ into sets ( $\mathbb{B}_{i}$ 's) containing $1999$ elements and the rest of the element be part of the set $\mathbb{A}$ Then the general solution of $G^{1999}(i)=i, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}$ is the following. If $x\in\mathbb{A}$ then $G(i)=i$ and $G(\mathbb{B}_{i})$ is a permutation of $\mathbb{B}_{i}$ which has no cycles less than $1999$ . So the only functions satisfying all the three give conditions are those that I noted in my previous post.
Actually I have found a more general function. Let $\mathbb{A}$ and $\mathbb{B}_{i}$ be non-intersecting sets whose union is $\mathbb{N}$ and for each $i$ we have $|\mathbb{B}_{i}|=1999$ Define the function $G$ as the following: If $x\in\mathbb{A}$ then $G(x)=x$ and $G(\mathbb{B}_{i})$ is a permutation of $\mathbb{B}_{i}$ such that there are no cycles smaller than $1999$ . Define the function $H$ as the following: $H(0)=0$ and if $x\in\mathbb{N}$ then $H(x)=1$ Define the function $I$ as mapping the prime numbers to natural numbers. Denote $p_{i}$ as being the $i^{th}$ prime number. Define the function $f$ as the following: $f\left(\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_{i}}\right)=\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{i})}$ $f$ satisfies the first condition
PROOFLet $m=\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_{i}}$ where $a_i$ are non-negative integers. From the definition of $G$ we get $G^{1999}(i)=i$ It is easy to get $H(H(a)b)=H(a)$ where $a\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ and $b\in\mathbb{N}$ $f^k\left(\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{i})}\right)=f^{k-1}\left(\prod_{i} p_{G^2(i)}^{H(H(a_{i})I(p_{i}))I(p_{G(i)})}\right)$ Now $H(a_{i})\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ and $I(p_{i})\in\mathbb{N}$ So $f^{k}\left(\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{i})}\right)=f^{k-1}\left(\prod_{i} p_{G^2(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{G(i)})}\right)$ Continuing this we get $f^{k}\left(\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{i})}\right)=\prod_{i} p_{G^{k+1}(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{G^k(i)})}$ So $f^{1999}\left(\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{i})}\right)=\prod_{i} p_{G^{2000}(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{G^{1999}(i)})}$ So $f^{2000}\left(\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_{i}}\right)=\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{H(a_{i})I(p_{i})}=f\left(\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_{i}}\right)$ So $f^{2000}(m)=f(m)$
$f$ satisfies the second condition
PROOFLet $m=\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_{i}}$ and $n=\prod_{i} p_{i}^{b_{i}}$ where $a_i$ and $b_i$ are non-negative integers. Then $mn=\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_{i}+b_{i}}$ and $gcd(m, n)=\prod_{i} p_{i}^{Min(a_{i}, b_{i})}$ It is easy to get $H(Max(a_{i}, b_{i}))=H(a_i+b_i)$ So $H(a_{i}+b_{i})+H(Min(a_{i}, b_{i}))=H(Max(a_{i}, b_{i}))+H(Min(a_{i}, b_{i}))=H(a_i)+H(b_i)$ So $f(mn)f(gcd(m, n))=\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{[H(a_i+b_i)+H(Min(a_{i}, b_{i}))]I(p_{i})}=\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{[H(a_i)+H(b_i)]I(p_{i})}$ So $f(mn)f(gcd(m, n))=\prod_{i} p_{G(i)}^{[H(a_i)+H(b_i)]I(p_{i})}=f(m)f(n)$
$f$ satisfies the third condition
PROOFLet $m=\prod_{i} p_{i}^{a_i}$ where $a_i$ are non-negative integers. $f(m)=1\iff H(a_i)I(p_i)=0, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}$ $I(p_i)>0, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}$ so $H(a_i)I(p_i)=0, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}\iff H(a_i)=0, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}$ $H(a_i)=0, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}\iff a_i=0, \forall i\in\mathbb{N}\iff m=1$ So $f(m)=1\iff m=1$

So those functions $f$ that I mentioned in my previous post also satisfy all the three given conditions. The more difficult part is to show that these are the only functions that $f$ could take or whether there are other forms. Has anyone got any ideas?

stem_md:
Find all primes  $p,q$  such that
\[p^q-q^p=pq^2-19\]
solution_md: $p^q\equiv p(mod q) \implies p\equiv -19(mod q) \implies \boxed{p+19\equiv 0(mod q)}$  $q^p\equiv q(mod p) \implies -q\equiv -19(mod q) \implies \boxed{19-q\equiv 0(mod p)}$ Now it's obvious that  $p=2$  or  $q=2$ **<u>1 case:</u>** $q=2 \implies 19-2=17\equiv 0(mod p) \implies p=17$  ,but after checking  $(p,q)=(17,2)$  is not a solution.**<u>2 case:</u>** $p=2 \implies 19+2=21\equiv 0(mod q) \implies q=3$  or  $q =7$ .Plug it in the given condition,it gives that the only solutions are  $(p,q)=(2,3),(2,7)$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Iran Contests/Pre-Preparation Course Examination/2007 Pre-Preparation Course Examination/359207.json

candidates:
From Fermat's little theorem we have  $p|q^p-q$  and  $q|p^q-p$ .
Thus in modulo  $p$  the equation is  $-q=-19 \implies p|q-19$ ; and in modulo  $q$  the equation is  $p=-19 \implies q|p+19$ .
We will suppose that  $19<q$ . Then  $p|q-19\implies p \le q-19$ . Also since  $q|p+19$  we have  $q\le p+19$ .
Then  $q\le p+19 \le (q-19)+19=q $  which implies equality throughout, i.e.  $q=p+19$ . By the parity difference one of  $p,q$  is even which implies  $p=2, q=21$  which is a contradiction.
Thus  $19>q$  so that  $q\in \{2,3,5,7,11,13\}$  so  $q-19\in \{-17, -16, -14,-12,-8,-6 \}$ , and  $p$  must be a prime divisor of an element of this set. $q=2 \implies p=17$  $q=3 \implies p=2$  $q=5 \implies p=2,7$  $q=7 \implies p=2,3$  $q=11 \implies p=2$  $q=13 \implies p=2,3$ Substituting these into the equation  $p^q-q^p=pq^2-19$ , we see that  $(2,7)$  is the only solution. :D

EDIT: yes  $(2,3)$  is also a solution.

stem_md:
$ R_k(m,n)$  is the least number such that for each coloring of  $ k$ -subsets of  $ \{1,2,\dots,R_k(m,n)\}$  with blue and red colors, there is a subset with  $ m$  elements such that all of its k-subsets are red or there is a subset with  $ n$  elements such that all of its  $ k$ -subsets are blue.
a) If we give a direction randomly to all edges of a graph  $ K_n$  then what is the probability that the resultant graph does not have directed triangles?
b) Prove that there exists a  $ c$  such that  $ R_3(4,n)\geq2^{cn}$ .
solution_md:
Working on that idea - what does a set of  $n$  in which every subset of three form an oriented transitive triple look like? It's a completely ordered set, in which each member beat those of higher rank and lost to those of lower rank.

Now, we need to build a tournament of  $k$  players in which the largest completely ordered subset is of size comparable to  $\log k$ . That sounds... doable. Taking the hint of the other question, let's go probabilistic. For convenience, let's call a completely ordered subset a "ladder".

Choose all  $\binom{k}{2}$  match results by coinflip. The probability that a given size  $n$  subset are completely ordered is  $2^{-\binom{n}{2}}\cdot n!$ . Over all such subsets, that gives us an expected number of  $\binom{k}{n}\cdot 2^{-\binom{n}{2}}\cdot n!$  size- $n$  ladders. If  $\left(2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\right)^n > k(k-1)\cdots (k-n+1)$ , this is less than  $1$  and there is some size- $k$  tournament with no size- $n$  ladders. Taking  $k=2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}$  here works.

By this and previous results,  $R_3(4,n)\ge 2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}$ .

This is not sharp. In all but the smallest of cases, you won't get sharp bounds for Ramsey numbers without enormous amounts of work. Clever construction could certainly do much better.

a) if \[ C_a(\pi)\equal{}\mbox{the number of cycles of length }a\mbox{ in }\pi\] then prove that  $ E(C_a(\pi))\equal{}\frac1a$ 
b) Prove that if  $ \{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k\}\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}$  the probability that  $ \pi$  does not have any cycle with lengths  $ a_1,\dots,a_k$  is at most  $ \frac1{\sum_{i\equal{}1}^ka_i}$
solution_md:
A permutation $ \pi$ is selected randomly through all $ n$ -permutations. a) if \[ C_a(\pi)=\mbox{the number of cycles of length }a\mbox{ in }\pi\] then prove that $ E(C_a(\pi))=\frac1a$ b) Prove that if $ \{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k\}\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ the probability that $ \pi$ does not have any cycle with lengths $ a_1,\dots,a_k$ is at most $ \frac1{\sum_{i=1}^ka_i}$
a) Let $K_n^a$ be the number of $n$ -permutations with no cycle with length $a$ . Then there are $\frac{1}{s!}\dbinom{n}{a,\dots,a,n-sa}(a-1)!^sK_{n-sa}=\frac{n!}{s!a^s}\frac{K_{n-sa}}{(n-sa)!}$ number of $\pi$ with $s$ cycles of length $a$ . So probability of having $s$ cycles of length $a$ is $\frac{1}{s!a^s}\frac{K_{n-sa}}{(n-sa)!}$ . Hence if $n=ma+r$ for some $0 \leq r\frac{1}{n}$ for $n\geq 3$ .

Let's introduce the indicator  $X_i$ , which is equal to 1, if the number  $i$  belongs to the cycle of length  $a$ . Then the expected value of the total number of cycles can be represented as  $E(C)=E(\sum_i X_i /a)=\sum E(X_i) /a$ . But  $X_i$  are identically distributed, so  $E(X_i)=E(X_1)$  and  $\sum E(X_i)=nE(X_1)$ . 

Going further we obtain that  $E(X_1)=P(X_1=1)$  and it is easy to show that it is equal to  $1/n$ . So we have  $E(C)=\frac{n}{na}=1/a$ .

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with  $AB=AC$ . Let point  $Q$  be on plane such that  $AQ \parallel BC$  and  $AQ = AB$ . Now let the  $P$  be the foot of perpendicular from  $Q$  to  $BC$ . Show that the circle with diameter  $PQ$  is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>easy bash</summary>Trivially,  $AQ$  touches  $(ABC)$  at A. Now, let us set  $BC$  and  $PQ$  as the  $x-axis$  and  $y-axis$  of the Cartesian plane respectively. Let us set  $AB = AC = AQ = a$ ,  $BC = b$ . Let  $D$  be the foot of perpendicular dropped from  $A$  on  $BC$ . Let  $AD = PQ = h$ . Then,  $P \equiv (0,0)$ ,  $Q \equiv (0,h)$ ,  $D \equiv (-a,0)$ ,  $A \equiv (-a,h)$ . Let  $X \equiv (0,\frac{h}{2})$  be the midpoint of  $PQ$  and let  $O$  be the center of  $(ABC)$ .
It can be written that  $\frac{a^{2}b}{4AO} = \frac{bh}{2}$  which implies  $AO = \frac{a^{2}}{2h}$ .

Again,  $A$  divides  $DO$  externally into the ratio of  $h:AO$ . So, if  $O \equiv (-a, y_1)$ , then  $\frac{hy_1}{h - AO} = h$  $\implies y_1 = h - AO = \frac{2h^{2} - a^{2}}{2h}$ Trivial calculations show that  $OX = \frac{a^{2} + h^{2}}{2h} = AO + QX$  which completes the proof. $Q.E.D.$</details>

stem_md: Assume that every root of polynomial  $P(x) = x^d - a_1x^{d-1} + ... + (-1)^{d-k}a_d$  is in  $[0,1]$ . Show that for every  $k = 1,2,...,d$  the following inequality holds: $ a_k - a_{k+1} + ... + (-1)^{d-k}a_d \geq 0 $
solution_md:
Assume that every root of polynomial $P(x) = x^d - a_1x^{d-1} + ... + (-1)^{d}a_d$ is in $[0,1]$ . Show that for every $k = 1,2,...,d$ the following inequality holds: $ a_k - a_{k+1} + ... + (-1)^{d-k}a_d \geq 0 $
In fact, it boils down to prove the following. Suppose all roots of $P(x)=a_0x^n + a_1 x^{n-1}+\dots + a_{n-1}x+a_n\,,\, a_0>0$ are in $(0,1)$ . Let $a'_k := a_n+a_{n-1}+\dots+a_k\,,\,k=0,1,\dots,n$ . Then $a'_0>0$ and the sequence $a'_0,a'_1,\dots,a'_n$ alternatively changes its sign. The idea is to apply a simple rational transformation which maps $(0,\infty)$ to $(0,1)$ after that the new polynomial would have all roots in $(0,\infty)$ . Then to apply the Descartes rule of signs. Let us set $x=\frac{1}{t+1}$ . Then all roots of the polynomial $Q(t)=a_n(t+1)^n+a_{n-1}(t+1)^{n-1}+\dots+a_1(t+1)+a_0$ are positive. The coefficient $b_k$ at $t^k$ of $Q(t)$ is: $$ b_{k}= a_n\binom{n}{k}+a_{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}+\dots+a_{k+1}\binom{k+1}{k}+ a_{k}\binom{k}{k}\,,\,k=0,1,\dots,n $$ Applying the Descartes rule of signs we get $b_0,b_1,\dots,b_n$ alternatively change its sign. Since $b_0=P(1)>0$ (because $a_0>0$ ), it yields: $$ (-1)^kb_k=(-1)^k \left[a_n\binom{n}{k}+a_{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}+\dots+a_{k+1}\binom{k+1}{k}+ a_{k}\binom{k}{k}\right]>0\,;\,k=0,1,\dots,n. $$ Obviously, adding consecutively to $(-1)^kb_k$ the terms $(-1)^{\ell}b_{\ell},\ell>k$ , multiplied by some coefficients we get $(-1)^k a'_k$ . That's: $$ (-1)^ka'_k = (-1)^kb_k + \sum_{\ell=k+1}^n \lambda_{\ell}(-1)^{\ell} b_{\ell}. $$ It remains to see $\lambda_{\ell}>0$ .

stem_md: 2. Let  $x_1, . . . , x_n$  be  $n$  integers, and let  $p$  be a positive integer, with  $p < n$ . Put  $$ S_1 = x_1 + x_2 + . . . + x_p $$    $$ T_1 = x_{p+1} + x_{p+2} + . . . + x_n $$    $$ S_2 = x_2 + x_3 + . . . + x_{p+1} $$    $$ T_2 = x_{p+2} + x_{p+3} + . . . + x_n + x_1 $$    $$ ... $$    $$ S_n=x_n+x_1+...+x_{p-1} $$    $$ T_n=x_p+x_{p+1}+...+x_{n-1} $$  For  $a = 0, 1, 2, 3$ , and  $b = 0, 1, 2, 3$ , let  $m(a, b)$  be the number of numbers  $i$ ,  $1 \leq i \leq n$ , such that  $S_i$  leaves remainder  $a$  on division by  $4$  and  $T_i$  leaves remainder  $b$  on division by  $4$ . Show that  $m(1, 3)$  and  $m(3, 1)$  leave the same remainder when divided by  $4$  if, and only if,  $m(2, 2)$  is even.
solution_md:
Let  $N= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ . Note that  $S_i+T_i = N$  is fixed.
Now if  $N \not= 0 \pmod{4}$ , we have  $m(1,3)=m(3,1)=m(2,2)=0$ . 
If  $4|N$ ,  $\sum_{i=1}^n S_i = pN \equiv 0 \equiv m(1,3)+3m(3,1)+2m(2,2) \equiv m(1,3)-m(3,1)+2m(2,2)$ . The result follows.  $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md: Let  $x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots$  be sequence of nonzero real numbers satisfying   $$ x_n=\frac{x_{n-2}x_{n-1}}{2x_{n-2}-x_{n-1}}, \quad \quad n=3,4,5,\dots $$   Establish necessary and sufficient conditions on  $x_1,x_2$  for  $x_n$  to be an integer for infinitely many values of  $n$ .
solution_md:
Let $x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots$ be sequence of nonzero real numbers satisfying $$ x_n=\frac{x_{n-2}x_{n-1}}{2x_{n-2}-x_{n-1}}, \quad \quad n=3,4,5,\dots $$ Establish necessary and sufficient conditions on $x_1,x_2$ for $x_n$ to be an integer for infinitely many values of $n$ .
Easy to show with induction that $x_n=\frac{x_1x_2}{(x_1-x_2)n+2x_2-x_1}$ Hence the answer $\boxed{x_1=x_2\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}}$

stem_md: The year  $1978$  was “peculiar” in that the sum of the numbers formed with the first two digits and the last two digits is equal to the number formed with the middle two digits, i.e.,  $19+78=97$ . What was the last previous peculiar year, and when will the next one occur?
solution_md:
No earlier years in the 1900's are peculiar; if  $19xy$  is peculiar, then  $19 + xy = 9x \Rightarrow x \in \{7,8\}$ .

In the 1800's, we have that 1868 is peculiar. No later years work, so 1868 was the next earliest year.

There are no peculiar years in the 2000's or 2100's. No years in the 2200's are peculiar, since if  $22xy$  is peculiar, then  $22 + xy = 2x$  which has no solutions. Similarly, no years in the 2300's are peculiar. In the 2400's, we have that 2417 is peculiar. So the answer is 1868 and 2417.

stem_md: Let  $0\le x\le 1$ . Show that if  $n$  is any positive integer, then   $$ (1+x)^n\ge (1-x)^n+2nx(1-x^2)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} $$  .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Subtracting  $(1-x)^n$  over, it suffices to show  $((1+x) - (1-x))(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (1+x)^{n-1-i} (1-x)^i ) \geq 2nx(1-x^2)^{\tfrac{n-1}{2}}$ . If  $x=0$ , this reduces to  $0\geq 0$ , which is true, so assuming  $x \neq 0$ , we divide by  $2x$  to get  $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (1+x)^{n-1-i} (1-x)^i  \geq n(1-x)^{\tfrac{n-1}{2}} (1+x)^{\tfrac{n-1}{2}}$ , or  $\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (1+x)^{n-1-i} (1-x)^i}{n}  \geq \sqrt[n]{(1+x)^{\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} } (1-x)^{\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} }} = (1+x)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} (1-x)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}$ , which is true by AM-GM, done.
Equality holds iff  $(1+x)^{n-1-i} (1-x)^i$  is constant for  $0 \leq i \leq n-1$ , which only happens when  $x=0$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Ireland Contests/Ireland National Math Olympiad/1988 Irish Math Olympiad/1520074.json

stem_md: If facilities for division are not available, it is sometimes convenient in determining the decimal expansion of  $1/a$ ,  $a>0$ , to use the iteration   $$ x_{k+1}=x_k(2-ax_k), \quad \quad k=0,1,2,\dots , $$   where  $x_0$  is a selected “starting” value. Find the limitations, if any, on the starting values  $x_0$ , in order that the above iteration converges to the desired value  $1/a$ .
solution_md:
The limitation is  $0< x_0 < \frac{2}{a} $ .
In this case, clearly  $0<x_1$ . Moreover,  $x_1 = \frac{1}{a} ax_0 (2-ax_0) \le \frac{1}{a}$ . By induction, one can easily show that  $n \ge 1 \implies 0 < x_n \le \frac{1}{a}$ . Since  $0 < x \le \frac{1}{a} \implies x(2-ax) \ge x$ , we have  $x_2 \ge x_1$ . Since  $x \mapsto x(2-ax)$  is increasing on the interval  $\left(0 ,\, \frac{1}{a} \right]$ , we have monotonicity  $x_1 \le x_2 \le x_3 \le \cdots$ . By the monotonicity and boundedness of  $x_n$ , we have limit of  $x_n$  at the unique fixed point of  $x \mapsto x(2-ax)$  on the interval, i.e.  $x= \frac{1}{a}$ .
Conversely, suppose  $x_0 \le 0 \vee \frac{2}{a} \le x_0$ . If either  $x_0 = 0$  or  $x_0 = \frac{2}{a}$ , we have  $x_n = 0$  for each  $n \ge 1$ . Otherwise, we have  $x_1 <0$ . But then, by induction again we have decreasing monotonicity;  $0 > x_1 > x_2 > \cdots$  so it cannot converges to the desired point; actually it diverges to negative infinity.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Ireland Contests/Ireland National Math Olympiad/1988 Irish Math Olympiad/1520075.json

Problem: A mathematical moron is given the values b; c; A for a triangle ABC and
is required to fi nd a. He does this by using the cosine rule $ a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bccosA$ and misapplying the low of the logarithm to this to get $ log a^2 = log b^2 + log c^2 - log(2bc cos A) $ He proceeds to evaluate the right-hand side correctly, takes the anti-logarithms
and gets the correct answer. What can be said about the triangle ABC?
solution_md:
This is Irish MO'1988.
Given  $ log a^{2}= log b^{2}+log c^{2}-log(2bc cos A) $ thus,  $\frac{b^2c^2}{2bc\cos A}=a^2$ Putting the value of  $\cos A$ , we get $\frac{bc}{a^2}=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{bc}$ which simplifies to: $(b-a)(c-a)=0$ Thus,  $b=a$  or  $c=a$  or  $a=b=c$ .
Peace.

Faustus.

stem_md:
A 3x3 magic square, with magic number  $m$ , is a  $3\times 3$  matrix such that the entries on each row, each column and each diagonal sum to  $m$ . Show that if the square has positive integer entries, then  $m$  is divisible by  $3$ , and each entry of the square is at most  $2n-1$ , where  $m=3n$ . An example of a magic square with  $m=6$  is

\[\left( \begin{array}{ccccc}
2 & 1 & 3
3 & 2 & 1
1 & 3 & 2
\end{array} \right)\]
solution_md:
let the sum of the four corner cells be  $c$ ,  the sum of the four 'edge' cells be  $e$ , and the middle cell be  $g$ .
Then, considering the two diagonals,  $c+2g=2m$ Considering the middle row and middle column,  $e+2g=2m$ And considering the total of all 9 cells,  $c+e+g=3m$ Adding the first two equations and subtracting the third gives  $m=3g$  Done.

So, for the inequality, we need to show each entry is at most 2g-1.  For the corner cells, this follows immediately from considering a diagonal, and for the edge cells, this follows from considering the middle row or column

2. Each of   $n$  members of a club is given a different item of information. The members are allowed to share the information, but, for security reasons, only in the following way: A pair may communicate by telephone. During a telephone call only one member may speak. The member who speaks may tell the other member all the information (s)he knows. Determine the minimal number of phone calls that are required to convey all the information to each of the members.

Hi, from my sketches I'm thinking the answer is  $2n-2$  but I dont know how to prove that this number of calls is the smallest. Can anyone enlighten me? Thanks
solution_md:
<details><summary>Hi</summary>This was a MODS potd.</details>
We claim the answer is  $2n-2$ . The construction is clear, in the first  $n-1$  moves everyone tells a person  $A$  their information, and in the next  $n-1$  moves  $A$  tells everyone everything.

We now prove this is optimal. Call someone "wise" if they have has full information. Firstly, clearly at least  $n-1$  moves are needed before someone is wise. After this has happened, we still need at least  $n-1$  moves until everyone is wise because each move can only increase the number of wise people by 1. Thus, at least
\[(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 \text{ moves are needed}\]
and we're done.  $\blacksquare$ .

candidates:
<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>If only one person knew any information that had to be conveyed and the others were clueless, how many calls would it take then?</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>After  $n-1$  calls, there's someone that hasn't called anyone. What does that mean?</details>

<details><summary>Full solution if the hints are not enough</summary>$2n-2$  is constructible by having person  $k$  call  $k+1$  for  $k = 1, 2, \ldots n-1$ , after which person  $n$  knows all the information ( $n-1$  calls). Then person  $n$  calls each person up and tells them, for  $n-1$  more calls.

To show at least  $2n-2$  calls are needed: After  $n-1$  calls, no matter how they are done, some person, WLOG person  $n$ , hasn't called anyone. In each subsequent call only one more person can learn person  $n$ 's information, and there are  $n-1$  people that need to know. So after the first  $n-1$  calls, you need at least  $n-1$  more calls for everyone to learn what person  $n$  knows. That gives  $2n-2$  as a lower bound.</details>
thanks MellowMelon!

This is a (easier version) of the famous "Gossiping Dons" problem; see e.g. [Béla Bollobás, The Art of Mathematics] P48. Each of $n\geq 4$ Oxford dons knows a different item of information. The dons are allowed to share information by telephone; both may speak. Determine the minimal number of phone calls that are required to convey all the information to each of the dons. Here the answer is $2n-4$ with quite a convoluted argument - maybe someone may find a simpler and shorter approach :)

We claim that the minimum number of phone calls is $2n-2$ . Checking confirms the cases $n \in \{1,2,3\}$ . **Claim 1.** There cannot have been less than $2n-2$ phone calls for $n \geq 4$ . *Proof.* Assume the contrary, ie., that there is some $n \geq 4$ such that the number of phone calls is less than or equal to $2n-3$ . By the well-ordering principle, we can choose the smallest such $n$ . Furthermore, there must exist a person, call him Bob, such that before the last phone call everyone, except Bob, knows everyone else's information. Additionally, in order for the rest to know Bob's information, Bob has to have made at least one phone call to some other during the sequence of calls. Take this sequence and ignore every call that involves Bob. In the end, everyone but Bob knows everyone else's, except Bob's information, while Bob remains clueless only knowing his information. The number of phone calls in the reduced sequence must also be less than or equal to $2n-3-2=2n-5$ . If we remove Bob, we have shown that for $n-1$ people we can make a sequence of at most $2n-5<2(n-1)-2$ phone calls. This contradicts the fact that $n$ was chosen to be minimal. Finally, this contradiction proves our claim. **Claim 2.** $2n-2$ phone calls is sufficient. *Proof.* A construction can be found inductively. Constructions are clear for cases $n \in \{1,2,3\}$ . Suppose that there is some $n \geq 3$ such that a group of $n$ people can make exactly $2n-2$ phone calls. Take a group of $n+1$ people. The first person calls the second. Consider everyone except the first person. By the induction hypothesis, they can make $2n-2$ phone calls and in the end, everyone except the first person knows everyone else's information. Then some of these people can call the first person. Hence everyone knows everyone else's information and it has taken exactly $1+2n-2+1=2(n+1)-2$ phone calls. By the principle of induction, we are done. :P
