stem_md: A sequence  $ (x_n)$  is given as follows:  $ x_0,x_1$  are arbitrary positive real numbers, and  $ x_{n\plus{}2}\equal{}\frac{1\plus{}x_{n\plus{}1}}{x_n}$  for  $ n \ge 0$ . Find  $ x_{1998}$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $ x_0 \equal{} a$  and  $ x_1 \equal{} b$ . 

Using the recursion formula yields:  $ x_2 \equal{} \dfrac{1 \plus{} b}{a}$ ,  $ x_3 \equal{} \dfrac{a \plus{} b \plus{} 1}{ab}$ ,  $ x_4 \equal{} \dfrac{1 \plus{} a}{b}$ ,  $ x_5 \equal{} a$ ,  $ x_6 \equal{} b$ . 

Since the recursion is a 2nd order recursion, and  $ (x_0,x_1) \equal{} (x_5,x_6)$ , we have  $ x_{n \plus{} 5} \equal{} x_{n}$  for all  $ n \ge 0$ . 

Therefore,  $ x_{1998} \equal{} x_{1993} \equal{} \cdots \equal{} x_{8} \equal{} x_{3} \equal{} \dfrac{x_0 \plus{} x_1 \plus{} 1}{x_0x_1}$ .</details>

stem_md: Show that there is a positive number in the Fibonacci sequence which is divisible by  $ 1000$ .
solution_md:
Show that there is a positive number in the Fibonacci sequence which is divisible by $ 1000$ .
Consider the sequence $ u_1 \equal{} 1$ , $ u_2 \equal{} 1$ and $ u_{n \plus{} 2} \equal{} u_{n \plus{} 1} \plus{} u_n\pmod {1000}$ There are at most $ 1,000,000$ possible couples of values $ (u_k,u_{k \plus{} 1})$ and so this sequence is periodic with period $ T$ . If $ u_k \equal{} u_{k \plus{} T}$ and $ u_{k \plus{} 1} \equal{} u_{k \plus{} 1 \plus{} T}$ for some $ k > 1$ , then obviously $ u_{k \minus{} 1} \equal{} u_{k \plus{} T \minus{} 1}$ and $ u_{k} \equal{} u_{k \plus{} T}$ and so the cycle involves $ u_1$ and $ u_2$ So $ u_{T \plus{} 1} \equal{} 1$ and $ u_{T \plus{} 2} \equal{} 1$ So $ u_T \equal{} 0$

solution_md:
The sequence $ u_n$ , $ n \equal{} 0,1,2,...$ is defined by $ u_0 \equal{} 0, u_1 \equal{} 1$ and for each $ n \ge 1$ , $ u_{n \plus{} 1}$ is the smallest positive integer greater than $ u_n$ such that $ \{ u_0,u_1,...,u_{n \plus{} 1} \}$ contains no three elements in arithmetic progression. Find $ u_{100}$ .

Solve the system of equations:
 $ y^2\equal{}(x\plus{}8)(x^2\plus{}2),$  $ y^2\minus{}(8\plus{}4x)y\plus{}(16\plus{}16x\minus{}5x^2)\equal{}0.$
solution_md:
Solve the system of equations: $ y^2 \equal{} (x \plus{} 8)(x^2 \plus{} 2),$ $ y^2 \minus{} (8 \plus{} 4x)y \plus{} (16 \plus{} 16x \minus{} 5x^2) \equal{} 0.$
$ y^2 \minus{} (8 \plus{} 4x)y \plus{} (16 \plus{} 16x \minus{} 5x^2)\equal{}[y\minus{}(4\plus{}5x)] \cdot [y\minus{}(4\minus{}x)]\equal{}0$ **Case 1:** $ y\equal{}4\plus{}5x$ , then $ y^2\equal{}(x\plus{}8)(x^2\plus{}2)\equal{}x^3\plus{}8x^2\plus{}2x\plus{}16$ $ \Leftrightarrow x(x\minus{}19)(x\plus{}2)\equal{}0$ $ \Leftrightarrow (x,y)\equal{}(0,4),(19,99),(\minus{}2,\minus{}6)$ as solutions. **Case 2:** $ y\equal{}4\minus{}x$ , then $ (4\minus{}x)^2\equal{}y^2\equal{}x^3\plus{}8x^2\plus{}2x\plus{}16$ $ \Leftrightarrow x(x\plus{}2)(x\plus{}5)\equal{}0$ $ \Leftrightarrow (x,y)\equal{}(0,4),(\minus{}2,6),(\minus{}5,9)$ as solutions. So $ (x,y)\equal{}(0,4),(19,99),(\minus{}2,\minus{}6),(\minus{}2,6),(\minus{}5,9)$ are the only solutions for the system of equations.

A function  $ f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$  satisfies: $ (a)$   $ f(ab)\equal{}f(a)f(b)$  whenever  $ a$  and  $ b$  are coprime; $ (b)$   $ f(p\plus{}q)\equal{}f(p)\plus{}f(q)$  for all prime numbers  $ p$  and  $ q$ .
Prove that  $ f(2)\equal{}2,f(3)\equal{}3$  and  $ f(1999)\equal{}1999.$
solution_md:
A function $ f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ satisfies: $ (a)$ $ f(ab) \equal{} f(a)f(b)$ whenever $ a$ and $ b$ are coprime; $ (b)$ $ f(p \plus{} q) \equal{} f(p) \plus{} f(q)$ for all prime numbers $ p$ and $ q$ . Prove that $ f(2) \equal{} 2,f(3) \equal{} 3$ and $ f(1999) \equal{} 1999.$
Let $ p$ an odd prime : $ 2,p$ coprime $ \implies$ $ f(2p)\equal{}f(2)f(p)$ but $ p$ prime $ \implies$ $ f(p\plus{}p)\equal{}f(p)\plus{}f(p)$ and so $ f(2)\equal{}2$ $ f(2\plus{}2)\equal{}2f(2)$ and so $ f(4)\equal{}4$ $ f(5)\equal{}f(3\plus{}2)\equal{}f(3)\plus{}f(2)\equal{}f(3)\plus{}2$ $ f(7)\equal{}f(5\plus{}2)\equal{}f(5)\plus{}f(2)\equal{}f(3)\plus{}4$ $ f(12)\equal{}f(3)f(4)\equal{}4f(3)$ $ f(12)\equal{}f(5\plus{}7)\equal{}f(5)\plus{}f(7)\equal{}2f(3)\plus{}6$ So $ 4f(3)\equal{}2f(3)\plus{}6$ and $ f(3)\equal{}3$ and so $ f(5)\equal{}5$ and $ f(7)\equal{}7$ $ 3$ and $ 5$ coprime $ \implies$ $ f(15)\equal{}f(3\times 5)\equal{}f(3)f(5)\equal{}15$ $ 13$ and $ 2$ primes $ \implies$ $ f(15)\equal{}f(13\plus{}2)\equal{}f(13)\plus{}f(2)$ $ \implies$ $ f(13)\equal{}13$ $ 11$ and $ 2$ primes $ \implies$ $ f(13)\equal{}f(11\plus{}2)\equal{}f(11)\plus{}f(2)$ $ \implies$ $ f(11)\equal{}11$ $ 11$ and $ 3$ coprime $ \implies$ $ f(33)\equal{}f(3\times 11)\equal{}f(3)f(11)\equal{}33$ $ 31$ and $ 2$ primes $ \implies$ $ f(33)\equal{}f(31\plus{}2)\equal{}f(31)\plus{}f(2)$ $ \implies$ $ f(31)\equal{}31$ $ 29$ and $ 2$ primes $ \implies$ $ f(31)\equal{}f(29\plus{}2)\equal{}f(29)\plus{}f(2)$ $ \implies$ $ f(29)\equal{}29$ $ 13$ and $ 2$ coprime $ \implies$ $ f(26)\equal{}f(2\times 13)\equal{}f(2)f(13)\equal{}26$ $ 23$ and $ 3$ primes $ \implies$ $ f(26)\equal{}f(23\plus{}3)\equal{}f(23)\plus{}f(3)\equal{}f(23)\plus{}3$ $ \implies$ $ f(23)\equal{}23$ $ 23$ and $ 29$ coprime $ \implies$ $ f(667)\equal{}f(23\times 29)\equal{}f(23)f(29)\equal{}667$ $ 667$ and $ 3$ coprime $ \implies$ $ f(2001)\equal{}f(3\times 667)\equal{}f(3)f(667)\equal{}2001$ $ 1999$ and $ 2$ primes $ \implies$ $ f(2001)\equal{}f(1999\plus{}2)\equal{}f(1999)\plus{}2$ $ \implies$ $ f(1999)\equal{}1999$

stem_md:
The sum of positive real numbers  $ a,b,c,d$  is  $ 1$ . Prove that:
 $ \frac{a^2}{a\plus{}b}\plus{}\frac{b^2}{b\plus{}c}\plus{}\frac{c^2}{c\plus{}d}\plus{}\frac{d^2}{d\plus{}a} \ge \frac{1}{2},$ 

with equality if and only if  $ a\equal{}b\equal{}c\equal{}d\equal{}\frac{1}{4}$ .
solution_md: This is a direct application of T2 Lemma, since notice that if  $a_{i} \in \{a,b,c,d\}, b_{1} \in \{a+b, b+c, c+d, d+a\}$  we get: $ \frac{a^2}{a+b}+\frac{b^2}{b+c}+\frac{c^2}{c+d}+\frac{d^2}{d+a} \ge \frac{(a+b+c+d)^2}{2(a+b+c+d)} = \frac{1}{2}$ . Equality holds when  $a_{1} = kb_{1}$  for  $1 \le i \le n$ , meaning that  $a+b+c+d = 2k(a+b+c+d) \iff k = \frac{1}{2}$ . Therefore,  $a = \frac{a+b}{2} \iff a = b$ , so doing this with all pairs  $(a_{i}, b_{i})$  we obtain the desired condition.  $\square$

stem_md: Find all positive integers  $ m$  with the property that the fourth power of the number of (positive) divisors of  $ m$  equals  $ m$ .
solution_md:
Find all positive integers $ m$ with the property that the fourth power of the number of (positive) divisors of $ m$ equals $ m$ .
As $ m$ is a fourth power, the question $ \Leftrightarrow m\equal{}p_1^{4a_1}p_2^{4a_2}...\equal{}[(4a_1\plus{}1)(4a_2\plus{}1)...]^4$ $ \Leftrightarrow p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...\equal{}(4a_1\plus{}1)(4a_2\plus{}1)...$ R.H.S. is odd $ \Rightarrow 2 \in p_i$ As for $ p_i>5$ , $ p_i>4a_i\plus{}1$ . So $ p_1\equal{}3$ or $ 5$ **Case 1:** $ p_1\equal{}5$ , then as for $ a_1 \ge 2$ we have $ 5^{a_1}>4a_1\plus{}1$ , and also if other larger primes are contained in $ p_i$ , R.H.S. will be smaller than L.H.S. So $ m\equal{}5^{4(1)}\equal{}625$ is the only solution for this case. **Case 2:** $ p_1\equal{}3$ , $ a_1\equal{}2$ , then for similar reason we connot contain primes $ >5$ and the power of $ 5 \le 1$ So $ m\equal{}3^{4(2)}\equal{}6561$ or $ m\equal{}3^{4(2)}5^{4(1)}\equal{}4100625$ are solutions for this case. **Case 3:** $ p_1\equal{}3$ , $ a_1\equal{}1$ , then $ (4 \times 1\plus{}1)\equal{}5|L.H.S. \Rightarrow p_2\equal{}5$ Now if $ a_2 \ge 2$ we have $ \frac{L.H.S.}{R.H.S.} \ge \frac{3^15^{a_2}}{5(4a_2\plus{}1)} \ge \frac{3^15^{2}}{5(4(2)\plus{}1)}>1$ , contardiction. And $ a_2\equal{}1$ doesn't gives a solution. so no solution for this case. **Case 4:** $ p_1\equal{}3$ , $ a_1>2$ , then $ L.H.S.>R.H.S.$ , no solution again. So $ m\equal{}625, 6561, 4100625$ are the only solutions.

stem_md: Let  $ f(x)\equal{}5x^{13}\plus{}13x^5\plus{}9ax$ . Find the least positive integer  $ a$  such that  $ 65$  divides  $ f(x)$  for every integer  $ x$ .

candidates:
$ 65\equal{}5\cdot13$  so we just need it to be divisible by both.
For divisiblity by  $ 5$  let's  assume  $ 5$  doesn't divide  $ x$ , then by Fermat's little theorem we need  $ 5|13x\plus{}9ax \Longrightarrow 5|1\plus{}3a$ 
Similarly we need  $ 13|5\plus{}9a$ . Now we just use Chinese Remainder theorem and find the least positive  $ a$ .

Another solution: $f(x)=5x^{13}-5x+5x+13x^{5}-13x+13x+9ax=5(x^{13}-x)+13(x^{5}-x)+9(a+2)x$ By Fermat's little theorem, we have  $x^{13}-x\equiv 0 \pmod {13}$ , so  $5(x^{13}-x)\equiv 0 \pmod{65}$  and  $x^{5}-x\equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ , so  $13(x^{5}-x)\equiv 0 \pmod{65}$ .  $65 \nmid 9$ , then  $65 \mid a+2$  and its easy to see that  $a=63$  is the solution.

stem_md:
The sequence  $ a_1<a_2<...<a_M$  of real numbers is called a weak arithmetic progression of length  $ M$  if there exists an arithmetic progression  $ x_0,x_1,...,x_M$  such that:
 $ x_0 \le a_1<x_1 \le a_2<x_2 \le ... \le a_M<x_M.$ 
 $ (a)$  Prove that if  $ a_1<a_2<a_3$  then  $ (a_1,a_2,a_3)$  is a weak arithmetic progression. $ (b)$  Prove that any subset of  $ \{ 0,1,2,...,999 \}$  with at least  $ 730$  elements contains a weak arithmetic progression of length  $ 10$ .
solution_md:
(b) We prove a stronger claim that any subset of  $ \{ 0,1,2, \ldots ,10^{n} - 1\}$  with at least  $9^n + 1$  elements contains a weak arithmetic progression of length  $10$  for all positive integers  $n.$  We do this by induction.

Base case:  $n = 1$  works, because the only subset of size  $10$  of  $\{0, 1, \ldots, 9\}$  is  $\{0, 1, \ldots, 9\}$  itself, which is clearly a weak arithmetic progression.

Inductive step: Suppose that the claim holds for  $n = k.$  Then, separate  $ \{ 0,1,2, \ldots ,10^{k+1} - 1\}$  into the  $10$  equal sized sets   $$ \{ 0,1,2, \ldots ,10^{k+1} - 1\} = \{ 0,1,2, \ldots ,10^{k} - 1\} \cup \{ 10^{k},10^{k} + 1,10^{k} + 2, \ldots , 2\cdot 10^{k} - 1\} \cup \ldots \cup \{ 9\cdot 10^{k},9\cdot 10^{k} + 1, 9\cdot 10^{k} + 2, \ldots , \cdot 10^{k+1} - 1\}. $$   By the Pigeonhole Principle, if we choose  $9^{k+1} + 1$  numbers from this, at least one subset will contain at least  $9^k + 1$  numbers. By the inductive hypothesis, that subset will contain a weak arithmetic progression, which completes the induction.

The problem is just this when  $n = 3.$

stem_md: Consider all parabolas of the form  $ y\equal{}x^2\plus{}2px\plus{}q$  for  $ p,q \in \mathbb{R}$  which intersect the coordinate axes in three distinct points. For such  $ p,q$ , denote by  $ C_{p,q}$  the circle through these three intersection points. Prove that all circles  $ C_{p,q}$  have a point in common.
solution_md:
I claim that the point  $(0, 1)$  is on all circles  $C_{p, q}$ .

    The circle  $C_{p, q}$  must pass through the three points
      $$     (-p-\sqrt{p^{2}-q}, 0), \quad (-p+\sqrt{p^{2}-q}, 0), \quad \text{and} \quad (0, q).
     $$      Some computation yields that the circle has the center  $O$  and radius  $r$  with
      $$     O = \left(-p, \frac{1 + q}{2}\right), \quad \text{and} \quad r = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{4 p^{2}+(q-1)^{2}}.
     $$      giving the equation of the circle 
      $$     (x + p)^2 + \left(y - \frac{1 + q}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{4p^2 + (q - 1)^2}{4}.
     $$      Letting  $x = 0$  and  $y = 1$  on the LHS gives
      $$     (p)^2 + \left(1 - \frac{1 + q}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{4p^2 + (q - 1)^2}{4},
     $$      so the point  $(0,1)$  lies on all circles  $C_{p, q}$ .

solution_md:
Prove that if $ x,y$ are nonnegative real numbers with $ x \plus{} y \equal{} 2$ , then: $ x^2 y^2 (x^2 \plus{} y^2) \le 2$ .
$ x\plus{}y\equal{}2$ and $ x,y\geq 0$ $ \implies$ $ xy\equal{}2x\minus{}x^2\leq 1$ $ x^2y^2(x^2\plus{}y^2)\minus{}2\equal{}x^2y^2((x\plus{}y)^2\minus{}2xy)\minus{}2$ $ \equal{}4x^2y^2\minus{}2x^3y^3\minus{}2$ $ \equal{}2(1\minus{}xy)(xy\minus{}\frac{1\plus{}\sqrt 5}{2})(xy\plus{}\frac{\sqrt 5\minus{}1}{2})$ $ \leq 0$ since $ 0\leq xy\leq 1$ Q.E.D.

 $ \equal{}\frac{(ad\plus{}bc)\sin A}{2}\equal{}\frac{(ad\plus{}bc)BD}{4R}\Rightarrow R\equal{}\frac{BD(ad\plus{}bc)}{4Q}$

stem_md:
For each positive integer  $ n$  find all positive integers  $ m$  for which there exist positive integers  $ x_1<x_2<...<x_n$  with:
 $ \frac{1}{x_1}\plus{}\frac{2}{x_2}\plus{}...\plus{}\frac{n}{x_n}\equal{}m.$
solution_md:
*Apologies if this is a bit sloppy, it's a late at night  :oops:*

    I claim that all positive integers  $m \leq \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$  can be written in this form.

    First, we prove that no larger value for  $m$  can be obtained,
    The maximum value of  $a/b$  for integers  $a$  and  $b$  occurs when  $b = 1$ . Thus
      $$     \frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{2}{x_{2}}+\frac{3}{x_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{n}{x_{n}} \leq 1  + 2 + 3 \cdots + n = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}.
     $$      
    Now we prove by induction that all such  $m$  can be obtained. For  $n = 1$ , the maximum is  $1$ , which can be obtained with  $x_1 = 1$ , so the base case is true.

    Then, assume that for some  $k$  there exists  $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k$  such that all  $m \leq \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$  can be obtained. 
    First, note that by adding the term
      $$     \frac{k + 1}{x_n},
     $$      we can still obtain any value in  $m$ , as if  $m \neq 1$ , we can write for some  $x_1, \dots, x_k$ ,
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{2}{x_{2}}+\frac{3}{x_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{k}{x_{k}} &= m - 1 
        \implies \frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{2}{x_{2}}+\frac{3}{x_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{k}{x_{k}} +\frac{k + 1}{x_{k+1}} &= m - 1 + \frac{k + 1}{x_{k+1}},
    \end{align*}
    so  $x_{k + 1} = k + 1$  gives the desired value for  $n$ . Otherwise, if  $m = 1$ , we can set  $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots x_{k + 1} = \frac{(k+1)(k + 2)}{2}$ .

    Now, to obtain all of the values in the range  $\frac{k(k + 1)}{2}$  to  $\frac{k(k + 1)}{2} + (k + 1)$ , we note that if we wish to obtain some value  $a$ , we can find 
      $$     \frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{2}{x_{2}}+\frac{3}{x_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{k}{x_{k}} = a - (k+1)
     $$      so long as  $1 \leq a - (k + 1) \leq \frac{k(k + 1)}{2}$ , 
    and then setting  $x_{k + 1} = 1$  gives
      $$     \frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{2}{x_{2}}+\frac{3}{x_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{k+1}{1} = a - (k + 1) + \frac{k+1}{1} = a,
     $$      so we can obtain all the values in that range, and so by induction, for any  $n$ , we can obtain any  $m \leq \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$

solution_md:
let the consecutive integers be  $ k,k\plus{}1\dots ,k\plus{}9$  let  $ k\equiv0\mod2$  (if the k is odd we do analogously)

stem_md: Find all positive integer solutions  $ (a,b,c,n)$  of the equation:  $ 2^n\equal{}a!\plus{}b!\plus{}c!$ .
solution_md:
Find all positive integer solutions $ (a,b,c,n)$ of the equation: $ 2^n \equal{} a! \plus{} b! \plus{} c!$ .
Wlog say $ a\geq b \geq c$ If $ c\geq 3$ , $ 3$ divides RHS but not LHS. So $ c<3$ 1) $ c\equal{}1$ Then $ b\equal{}1$ and $ a>1$ else RHS would be odd while LHS even. So $ 2^n\equal{}a!\plus{}2$ If $ n\equal{}1$ , this equation has no solution If $ n\equal{}2$ , we get the solution $ 2^2\equal{}2!\plus{}1!\plus{}1!$ If $ n>2$ , $ a<4$ else $ LHS\equal{}0\pmod 4$ while $ RHS\equal{}2\pmod 4$ . And we get the solution $ 2^3\equal{}3!\plus{}1!\plus{}1!$ 2) $ c\equal{}2$ Then $ 2^n\equal{}a!\plus{}b!\plus{}2\geq 6$ and so $ n\geq 3$ If $ b\geq 4$ , then $ LHS\equal{}0\pmod 4$ while $ RHS\equal{}2\pmod 4$ . So $ b<4$ 2.1) $ c\equal{}2$ and $ b\equal{}2$ Then $ 2^n\equal{}a!\plus{}4$ . If $ a\geq 4$ , $ RHS\equal{}4\pmod 8$ and so $ n<3$ and so no solution We just have to test $ a\in[2,3]$ and no solution. 2.2) $ c\equal{}2$ and $ b\equal{}3$ Then $ 2^n\equal{}a!\plus{}8$ If $ a\geq 8$ , $ RHS\equal{}8\pmod 16$ and so $ n<4$ and so no solution We just have to test $ a\in[3,7]$ and two solutions : $ 2^5\equal{}4!\plus{}3!\plus{}2!$ $ 2^7\equal{}5!\plus{}3!\plus{}2!$ So 4 solutions : $ 2^2\equal{}2!\plus{}1!\plus{}1!$ $ 2^3\equal{}3!\plus{}1!\plus{}1!$ $ 2^5\equal{}4!\plus{}3!\plus{}2!$ $ 2^7\equal{}5!\plus{}3!\plus{}2!$

stem_md: Let  $ ABC$  be a triangle with sides  $ BC\equal{}a, CA\equal{}b,AB\equal{}c$  and let  $ D$  and  $ E$  be the midpoints of  $ AC$  and  $ AB$ , respectively. Prove that the medians  $ BD$  and  $ CE$  are perpendicular to each other if and only if  $ b^2\plus{}c^2\equal{}5a^2$ .
solution_md:
Let  $A=(0,2p)$ ,  $B=(2q,0)$  and  $C=(2r,0)$ . Then  $D=(r,p)$  and  $E=(q,p)$ , so  $B-D=(2q-r,-p)$  and  $C-E=(2r-q,-p)$ . Hence  $(B-D)\cdot (C-E)=(2q-r)(2r-q)+p^2$ .
On the other hand, we have  $a^2=4(q-r)^2$ ,  $b^2=4(r^2+p^2)$  and  $c^2=4(q^2+p^2)$ , so  $b^2+c^2-5a^2=4(r^2+p^2)+4(q^2+p^2)-20(q-r)^2$ . Hence  $8(B-D)\cdot (C-E)=b^2+c^2-5a^2$ . Therefore\begin{align*}BD\perp CE & \iff (B-D)\cdot (C-E)=0 
& \iff 8(B-D)\cdot (C-E)=0 
& \iff b^2+c^2-5a^2=0 
& \iff b^2+c^2=5a^2,
\end{align*}as desired.

stem_md:
Show that if an odd prime number  $ p$  can be expressed in the form  $ x^5\minus{}y^5$  for some integers  $ x,y,$  then:
 $ \sqrt{\frac{4p\plus{}1}{5}}\equal{}\frac{v^2\plus{}1}{2}$  for some odd integer  $ v$ .
solution_md:
Show that if an odd prime number $ p$ can be expressed in the form $ x^5 \minus{} y^5$ for some integers $ x,y,$ then: $ \sqrt {\frac {4p \plus{} 1}{5}} \equal{} \frac {v^2 \plus{} 1}{2}$ for some odd integer $ v$ .
$ p>0 \Rightarrow x>y$ $ p\equal{}x^5\minus{}y^5\equal{}(x\minus{}y)(x^4\plus{}x^3y\plus{}x^2y^2\plus{}xy^3\plus{}y^4)$ is a prime. $ x^4\plus{}x^3y\plus{}x^2y^2\plus{}xy^3\plus{}y^4\equal{}(x\plus{}y)(x^3\plus{}y^3)\plus{}x^2y^2\equal{}1 \Rightarrow x\equal{}1,y\equal{}\minus{}1 \Rightarrow p\equal{}2$ , contradiction. $ x^4\plus{}x^3y\plus{}x^2y^2\plus{}xy^3\plus{}y^4\equal{}(x\plus{}y)(x^3\plus{}y^3)\plus{}x^2y^2\equal{}\minus{}1 \Rightarrow$ no solution. So we must have $ x\minus{}y\equal{}1$ , $ p\equal{}(y\plus{}1)^5\minus{}y^5\equal{}5y^4\plus{}10y^3\plus{}10y^2\plus{}5y\plus{}1$ $ \sqrt {\frac {4p \plus{} 1}{5}} \equal{} \sqrt{4y^4\plus{}8y^3\plus{}8y^2\plus{}4y\plus{}1}\equal{}2y^2\plus{}2y\plus{}1\equal{}\frac{(2y\plus{}1)^2\plus{}1}{2}$ , done.

stem_md: Prove that for all positive integers  $ n$ :  $ \frac{2n}{3n\plus{}1} \le \displaystyle\sum_{k\equal{}n\plus{}1}^{2n}\frac{1}{k} \le \frac{3n\plus{}1}{4(n\plus{}1)}$ .
solution_md:
Prove that for all positive integers $ n$ : $ \frac {2n}{3n \plus{} 1} \le \displaystyle\sum_{k \equal{} n \plus{} 1}^{2n}\frac {1}{k} \le \frac {3n \plus{} 1}{4(n \plus{} 1)}$ .
We have, for $ 0 < a < x \le y$ , $ \frac {1}{x} \plus{} \frac {1}{y} < \frac {1}{x \minus{} a} \plus{} \frac {1}{y \plus{} a}$ $ \Leftrightarrow (x \minus{} a)(y \plus{} a) < xy \Leftrightarrow 0 < a(y \minus{} x \plus{} a)$ , which is obviously true. So, $ \frac {2n}{3n \plus{} 1} \equal{} \frac {n}{2}(\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{2n \plus{} (n \plus{} 1)}{2}} \plus{} \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{2n \plus{} (n \plus{} 1)}{2}})$ $ \le \sum_{k \equal{} n \plus{} 1}^{2n}\frac {1}{k} \le \frac {n}{2}(\frac {1}{n \plus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {1}{2n})$ Now $ \frac {n}{2}(\frac {1}{n \plus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {1}{2n}) \equal{} \frac {3n \plus{} 1}{4(n \plus{} 1)}$ $ \Leftrightarrow n(\frac {2(n \plus{} 1)}{n \plus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {2(n \plus{} 1)}{2n}) \equal{} 3n \plus{} 1$ , which is obviously true, done. Equality for left equality holds $ \Leftrightarrow n \equal{} 1$ Equality for right equality holds $ \Leftrightarrow n \equal{} 1,2$

stem_md: Find the least positive integer  $ a$  such that  $ 2001$  divides  $ 55^n\plus{}a \cdot 32^n$  for some odd  $ n$ .
solution_md:
Find the least positive integer $ a$ such that $ 2001$ divides $ 55^n \plus{} a \cdot 32^n$ for some odd $ n$ .
$ 2009\equal{}3\cdot23\cdot29.$ $ 55^n\equiv 1\pmod3$ , $ 32^n\equiv(\minus{}1)^n\equiv\minus{}1\pmod3$ . So $ 1\equiv a\pmod3$ . $ 55\equiv32\pmod{23}$ . So $ 55^n\plus{}a\cdot32^n\equiv(a\plus{}1)\cdot32^n\pmod{23}$ . So $ 23$ must divide $ (a\plus{}1)32^n$ , which is equvalent to $ a\equiv\minus{}1\pmod{23}$ $ 55\equiv\minus{}32\pmod{29}$ . So $ 55^n\plus{}a\cdot32^n\equiv(a\minus{}1)\cdot32^n\pmod{29}$ . So $ a\equiv1\pmod{29}$ So $ a$ must be the smallest natural number s.t. $ a\equiv1\pmod3$ , $ a\equiv\minus{}1\pmod{23}$ , $ a\equiv1\pmod{29}$ So $ a\equal{}436$

stem_md: Find all nonnegative real numbers  $ x$  for which  $ \sqrt[3]{13\plus{}\sqrt{x}}\plus{}\sqrt[3]{13\minus{}\sqrt{x}}$  is an integer.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $ N \equal{} \sqrt[3]{13\plus{}\sqrt{x}}\plus{}\sqrt[3]{13\minus{}\sqrt{x}}$ . 

Note that  $ N > \sqrt[3]{\sqrt{x}}\plus{}\sqrt[3]{\minus{}\sqrt{x}} \equal{} 0$ . 

Cubing both sides yields:  $ N^3 \equal{} (13\plus{}\sqrt{x})\plus{}$   $ 3\left(\sqrt[3]{13\plus{}\sqrt{x}}\right)\left(\sqrt[3]{13\minus{}\sqrt{x}}\right)\left(\sqrt[3]{13\plus{}\sqrt{x}}\plus{}\sqrt[3]{13\minus{}\sqrt{x}}\right)$   $ \plus{}(13\minus{}\sqrt{x})$   $ N^3 \equal{} 26\plus{}3\left(\sqrt[3]{169\minus{}x}\right)N$   $ \sqrt[3]{169\minus{}x} \equal{} \dfrac{N^3\minus{}26}{3N}$   $ x \equal{} 169 \minus{} \left(\dfrac{N^3\minus{}26}{3N}\right)^3 > 0$  

It is easy to see that if  $ N \ge 5$ , then  $ x < 0$ . 

Therefore,  $ N \in \{ 1,2,3,4 \}$ .  $ N\equal{}1$  yields  $ x \equal{} \dfrac{20188}{27} \equal{} 747 \frac{19}{27}$   $ N\equal{}2$  yields  $ x \equal{} 196$   $ N\equal{}3$  yields  $ x \equal{} \dfrac{123200}{729} \equal{} 168 \frac{168}{169}$   $ N\equal{}4$  yields  $ x \equal{} \dfrac{29645}{216} \equal{} 137 \frac{53}{216}$</details>

stem_md:
Determine all functions  $ f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$  which satisfy:
 $ f(x\plus{}f(y))\equal{}f(x)\plus{}y$  for all  $ x,y \in \mathbb{N}$ .
solution_md:
Setting  $x = y = 0$  gives
      $$     f(0 + f(0)) = f(0) + 0 \implies f(f(0)) = f(0).
     $$      Then  $x = 0$ ,  $y = f(0)$  gives
      $$     f(f(f(0))) = f(f(0)) = 2f(0) = f(0),
     $$      so  $f(0) = 0$ . Then  $x = 0$  gives  $f(f(y)) = y$ , and so
     $y = f(y)$  gives 
      $$     f(x + f(f(y))) = f(y) + f(x) = f(x + y),
     $$      which is Cauchy's functional equation which over the positive integers only has the solution  $f(x) = ax$ . Substituting back into the equation, we find that only  $a = 1$  works, and the only such function  $f$  is  $f(x) = x$ .

stem_md: $ (a)$  A group of people attends a party. Each person has at most three acquaintances in the group, and if two people do not know each other, then they have a common acquaintance in the group. What is the maximum possible number of people present? $ (b)$  If, in addition, the group contains three mutual acquaintances, what is the maximum possible number of people?
solution_md:
a) Consider a given person Siddhant. If he does not know seven or more people, then he either has more than three acquaintances or one of his acquaintances has more than three acquaintances, so the maximum number of people is  $ 1 \plus{} 3 \plus{} 6 \equal{} 10$ . Example should be easy to construct.

b) Here, none of the people in the triangle can know more than one other person. So let one of them, Siddhant, know Stephen Wolfram. Then the other two can each know at most one person, and we can have Stephen Wolfram have two more acquaintances by acquainting them to the two people we just constructed. The answer is thus  $ 8$ , and the example I already essentially gave.

stem_md:
Find all triples of positive integers  $ (p,q,n)$ , with  $ p$  and  $ q$  primes, satisfying:
 $ p(p\plus{}3)\plus{}q(q\plus{}3)\equal{}n(n\plus{}3)$ .
solution_md:
Here is my solution.
By  $ mod \ 3$ , we have  $ p^2 \plus{} q^2 \equiv \ n^2$ . Hence,  $ p$  or  $ q$  is equal to  $ 3$ , otherwise  $ n^2 \equiv \ 2$ . Now, w.l.o.g. suppose that  $ p \equal{} 3$ , so the equation becomes  $ 18 \plus{} q(q \plus{} 3) \equal{} n(n \plus{} 3)$ . Solving like a 2-nd degree equation in  $ n$ , we have the discriminant equals to  $ \Delta \equal{} \sqrt {4q(q \plus{} 3) \plus{} 81}$ . Since  $ n$  is a integer and  $ \Delta$  is odd,  $ 4q(q \plus{} 3) \plus{} 81 \equal{} (2k \plus{} 1)^2$ , where  $ k$  is a nonnegative integer. Hence  $ q(q \plus{} 3) \equal{} (k \minus{} 4)(k \plus{} 5)$ . 
Now suppose that  $ k \equal{} qt \minus{} 5$ , where  $ t$  is a nonnegative integer. So  $ q \plus{} 3 \equal{} (qt \minus{} 9)t$ . So  $ q \plus{} 3\geq qt \minus{} 9$ , so  $ t\leq \frac{q\plus{}12}{q}$ , and it's easy to see that  $ t\leq 7$ . By brute force, we can observe that  $ t \equal{} 5$  and  $ p \equal{} 2$ . Substituting in the equation, the only positive integer  $ n$  is  $ 4$ .
Analogously, the case  $ k \equal{} qt \plus{} 4$  don't generate solutions.
The unique triple  $ (p,q,n)$  is  $ (2,3,4)$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ 0<a,b,c<1$ . Prove the inequality:
 $ \frac{a}{1\minus{}a}\plus{}\frac{b}{1\minus{}b}\plus{}\frac{c}{1\minus{}c} \ge \frac {3 \sqrt[3]{abc}}{1\minus{} \sqrt[3]{abc}}.$ 

Determine the cases of equality.
solution_md:
Let  $f(x)=\frac{x}{1-x}$  furthermore  $f'(x)=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}\text{ and }f''(x)=\frac{2}{(1-x)^3}>0, \forall x\in(0,1)$  thus  $f$  is convex for  $x\in(0,1)$ Now  $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a}{1-a}=\sum_{cyc}f(a)\overset{\text{Jensen}}{\ge}3f\left(\frac{\sum_{cyc}a}{3}\right)=\frac{3\sum_{cyc}a}{3-\sum_{cyc}a}$ Therefore the inequity is equal to  $\frac{3\sum_{cyc}a}{3-\sum_{cyc}a}\ge\frac{3\sqrt[3]{abc}}{1-\sqrt[3]{abc}}\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{cyc}a-\sqrt[3]{abc}\sum_{cyc}a\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}-\sqrt[3]{abc}\sum_{cyc}a$  
This transforms into  $\sum_{cyc}a\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}$  which is just  $\text{AM-GM}$   $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md: A  $ 3 \times n$  grid is filled as follows. The first row consists of the numbers from  $ 1$  to  $ n$  arranged in ascending order. The second row is a cyclic shift of the top row:  $ i,i\plus{}1,...,n,1,2,...,i\minus{}1$  for some  $ i$ . The third row has the numbers  $ 1$  to  $ n$  in some order so that in each of the  $ n$  columns, the sum of the three numbers is the same. For which values of  $ n$  is it possible to fill the grid in this way? For all such  $ n$ , determine the number of different ways of filling the grid.
solution_md:
Let the cycle be  $ x_i$  and the permutation  $ y_i$ . We have  $ \sum i\plus{}x_i\plus{}y_i\equal{}3\binom{n\plus{}1}{2}$  so that  $ i\plus{}x_i\plus{}y_i\equal{}3(n\plus{}1)/2$ , so  $ n$  is odd.

The example is trivial enough; start  $ x_i$  at  $ \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ , start  $ b_i$  at  $ n$  and cycle down through the odds, then start over again at the highest even.

stem_md:
Suppose  $ n$  is a product of four distinct primes  $ a,b,c,d$  such that: $ (i)$   $ a\plus{}c\equal{}d;$  $ (ii)$   $ a(a\plus{}b\plus{}c\plus{}d)\equal{}c(d\minus{}b);$  $ (iii)$   $ 1\plus{}bc\plus{}d\equal{}bd$ .
Determine  $ n$ .
solution_md:
Full solution:

    Equation (a) implies that  $a < d$  and  $c < d$ , and also as  $d$  must be odd, we must have either  $a = 2$  or  $c = 2$ .
    Then, the RHS of equation (c) implies that the LHS is odd, so we must have  $bc$  being odd, so  $c \neq 2$  and  $a = 2$ .
    
    So  $d = c + 2$ , and substituting into (c) we have
      $$     1 + bc + (c + 2) = b(c + 2) \implies c = 2b - 3
     $$      and using (b),
      $$     2(2 + b + c + (c + 2)) = c((c + 2) - b) \implies 2(2 + b + 2(2b - 3) + 2) = (2b - 3)((2b - 3) + 2 - b),
     $$      and solving yields  $b = \frac{1}{2}$  or  $b = 7$ , so as  $b$  is prime,  $b = 7$ , then  $c = 11$  and  $d = 13$ .
    
    Multiplying,  $n = 2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 = 2002$ .

stem_md:
Find all functions  $ f: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$  such that:
 $ f(x\plus{}f(y))\equal{}y\plus{}f(x)$  for all  $ x,y \in \mathbb{Q}$ .
solution_md:
Slightly different but a very similar solution:

I claim that  $f(x) = x$  and  $f(x) = -x$  are the only solutions.
    
    Let  $x = 0$ . Then
      $$     f(f(y)) = y + f(0).
     $$      Setting  $y = f(0 - f(0))$  gives
      $$     f(x + f(f(0 - f(0)))) = f(x + 0 - f(0) + f(0)) = f(x) = f(0 - f(0)) + f(x),
     $$      thus  $f(0 - f(0)) = 0$ , and  $f(f(0 - f(0))) = 0 = f(0)$ , so  $f(0) = 0$ .
    This implies that  $f(f(y)) = y$ .

    Finally, with  $x = a$  and  $y = f(b)$ , we have
      $$     f(a + f(f(b))) = f(a + b) = f(b) + f(a),
     $$      which is Cauchy's equation, and over  $\mathbb{Q}$  has only the solution  $f(x) = kx$  for some  $k \in \mathbb{Q}$ .
    Substituting, we find that only  $k = \pm 1$  works, so the only solutions are  $f(x) = x$  and  $f(x) = -x$ , both of which are valid.

stem_md: Let  $ \alpha\equal{}2\plus{}\sqrt{3}$ . Prove that  $ \alpha^n\minus{}[\alpha^n]\equal{}1\minus{}\alpha^{\minus{}n}$  for all  $ n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Rewrite the identity as:  $ \alpha^{n} \plus{} \alpha^{ \minus{} n} \equal{} \lfloor\alpha^{n}\rfloor \plus{} 1$  

For  $ n \equal{} 0$ , this becomes  $ 1 \plus{} 1 \equal{} [1] \plus{} 1 \Rightarrow 2 \equal{} 2$  which is true. 

Note that  $ \alpha^{ \minus{} 1} \equal{} 2 \minus{} \sqrt {3}$ . 

The identity becomes:  $ (2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n \plus{} (2 \minus{} \sqrt {3})^n \equal{} [(2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n] \plus{} 1$  

It is easy to see that for all  $ n \in \mathbb{N}$ ,  $ (2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n \plus{} (2 \minus{} \sqrt {3})^n$  is an integer,  $ (2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n$  is not an integer, and  $ 0 < (2 \minus{} \sqrt {3})^n < 1$ . 

Therefore,  $ (2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n \plus{} (2 \minus{} \sqrt {3})^n \equal{} \lceil(2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n\rceil \equal{} \lfloor(2 \plus{} \sqrt {3})^n\rfloor \plus{} 1$  as desired.</details>

    \begin{align*}
        AD^2 &= CD^2 + b^2 - 2b\cdot CD\cdot \cos C 
        BC^2 &= CE^2 + a^2 - 2a\cdot CD\cdot \cos C
    \end{align*}
    Thus as  $CD = CE$ ,
      $$ AD^2 - BC^2 = b^2 - a^2 + 2a\cdot CD\cdot \cos C - 2b\cdot CD\cdot \cos C = (b - a)(b + a -2\cdot CD \cdot \cos C).
     $$      Using  $CD = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - c)$ ,
      $$     AD^2 - BC^2 = (b - a)(b + a - (a + b - c) \cos C).
     $$      We have  $\cos C$  bounded as  $-1 \leq \cos C \leq 1$ , and as  $a + b - c > 0$  by the triangle inequality,
      $$     (b - a)c \leq AD^2 - BC^2  \leq (b - a)(2b + 2a - c)\leq 2.
     $$      If  $b = a$ , then this inequality holds. 
    Now assume that  $b > a$ . We wish to satisfy
      $$     (b - a)c \leq 2.
     $$      However, as the sidelengths of  $ABC$  are integers, we must have  $b = 2$ ,  $a = 1$  and  $c = 1$  or  $c = 2$ .

    If  $c = 1$ , the triangle inequality  $a + c > b \iff 2 > 2$  is not satisfied, so  $ABC$  is not a triangle. Similarly, if  $c = 2$ , then we have equality of  $(b - a)c = 2$ , which implies that  $\cos C = 1$  and  $C = 0$ , so  $ABC$  is also not a triangle.
    Thus, if a triangle with integer sidelengths satisfies  $\left| A D^{2}-B E^{2}\right| \leq 2,$  then  $AC = BC$  as required.

stem_md: (a) In how many ways can  $1003$  distinct integers be chosen from the set  $\{1, 2, ... , 2003\}$  so that no two of the chosen integers differ by  $10?$ (b) Show that there are  $(3(5151) + 7(1700)) 101^7$  ways to choose  $1002$  distinct integers from the set  $\{1, 2, ... , 2003\}$  so that no two of the chosen integers differ by  $10.$
solution_md: a. We can split the set  $\{1,2,...,2003\}$  into the 1003 sets  $\{1,11\},\{2,12\},...,\{10,20\},\{21,31\},\{22,32\},...,\{1990,2000\},\{2001\},\{2002\},\{2003\}$ .  We can pick at most one number from each set, so in fact we must pick exactly one number from each set.  Thus, we must have  $2001,2002,2003$  in our list of 1003 integers.  This also fixes our choices from the sets  $\{1981,1991\},\{1982,1992\},\{1983,1993\}$  as  $1981,1982,1983$ .  Continuing in this fashion we must include every integer congruent to  $1,2,$  or  $3$  mod  $20$ .  Now, look at the sets  $\{4,14\},...,\{10,20\}$ .  If we pick the lower number in any of these sets, we may pick either number in the corresponding set in the integers 21-40.  If we pick the larger number, all other choices are fixed for that number modulo 10.  Thus, for each digit 4,5,...,0, we only really care about the first set in which we choose the larger number.  It could never happen, or that first set could be any of  $100$  choices, so there are 101 distinct ways to choose integers congruent to each of 4,5,...,0 mod 10, so the total number of choices is  $101^7$ .

stem_md:
If  $a,b,c$  are the sides of a triangle whose perimeter is equal to 2 then prove that: 

a)  $abc+\frac{28}{27}\geq ab+bc+ac$ ; 

b)  $abc+1<ab+bc+ac$ 


See also [http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=47939&view=next](http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=47939&view=next)  (problem 1)

 :)
solution_md:
$1 < ab + bc + ac - abc \leq \frac{28}{27}$ Notice that  $(1-a)(1-b)(1-c) = 1 - (a+b+c) + ab + bc + ac - abc = -1 + ab + bc + ac - abc$ . Therefore, if we substract  $1$  from all sides of the inequality, we get $0 < (1-a)(1-b)(1-c) \leq \frac{1}{27}$ The left inequality is clearly true because of the triangle inequality ( $0 < a,b,c < 1$ ).
Now, we use Ravi-substitution where we write  $a = x+y, b=y+z, c = x+z$  with  $0 < x,y,z < 1$  and  $x+y+z = 1$ .
We get that  $(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)  = xyz \leq \frac{1}{27}$ Which is true by AM-GM.

stem_md: $A$  and  $B$  are distinct points on a circle  $T$ .  $C$  is a point distinct from  $B$  such that  $|AB|=|AC|$ , and such that  $BC$  is tangent to  $T$  at  $B$ . Suppose that the bisector of  $\angle ABC$  meets  $AC$  at a point  $D$  inside  $T$ . Show that  $\angle ABC>72^\circ$ .
solution_md:
Let O be the center of circle  $T$ , and let X be the intersection of AC and the angle bisector of  $ABC$ . 

Let  $\alpha=\angle XBC=\angle XBA$ . Since  $AB=AC$ ,   $$ \angle ACB=\angle ABC=2\alpha $$   so  $\angle AXB=3\alpha$ Since BC is a tangent,   $$ \angle OBC=90\implies \angle AOB=180-2\angle OBA=180-2(90-2\alpha)=4\alpha $$  In order for  $X$  to lie inside circle  $T$ ,  $\angle AXB$  must be greater than half of  $360-\angle AOB$  (this is essentially the  $180^\circ\le \angle AOB <360^\circ$ )

In other words,  $3\alpha>\frac{360-4\alpha}{2}\implies \alpha>36$ Since  $\alpha$  is half of  $\angle ABC$ , this means  $\angle ABC>72^\circ$

stem_md: Suppose  $p,q$  are distinct primes and  $S$  is a subset of  $\{1,2,\dots ,p-1\}$ . Let  $N(S)$  denote the number of solutions to the equation   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{q}x_i\equiv 0\mod p $$  where  $x_i\in S$ ,  $i=1,2,\dots ,q$ . Prove that  $N(S)$  is a multiple of  $q$ .
solution_md:
someone check if I'm wrong.
We prove the claim by induction on  $n=|S|$ .
base case  $n=1$  is trivial( $N(S)=0$ )
now suppose that the claim holds for  $S$  with  $|S|=n$ .we add a new member  $a$  to  $S$ .Call the new set  $S'$ .
note that  $N(S')=N(S)+k$  where  $k$  is the number of answers to the equation  $\sum_{i=1}^{q}x_i\equiv 0\mod p$  such that at least one of  $x_i$  s is  $a$ .
consider an answer  $(a,a,\cdots a,x_1,\cdots x_m)$  where  $a$  appears  $l$  times.changing the order of the variables gives us new answers so with these variables,we have  $\binom{q}{l} *M$  answers,where  $M$  is all the permutations of  $x_1,\cdots x_m$ .it's well-known that for prime  $q$  and  $l<q$  we have  $q| \binom{q}{l}$ ,so the number of answers having at least one  $a$  is divisible by  $q$  and so  $q|k$  and the induction is complete.

stem_md:
Each of the players in a tennis tournament played one match against each of
the others. If every player won at least one match, show that there is a group
A; B; C of three players for which A beat B, B beat C and C beat A.
solution_md: Let  $P_1,..P_n$  be the n players.  $P_i>P_j$  if and only if  $P_i$  beats  $P_j$ , We must find a pair  $(P_i,P_j,P_k)$  such that  $P_i>P_j>P_k>P_i$ . Suppose we don't have such a pair so choosing  $P_i> P_j >P_k$ , we also have  $P_i>P_k$ . In other words, every player  $P_i$  who beats another player  $P_j$  beats all the players defeated by  $P_j$ . Now, it's easy to finish considering the one who has the less wins, let him be  $P_l$ , but he defeated  $P_r$ , so  $P_l$  defeated  $P_r$  and all the people defeated by  $P_r$ , so  $P_r$  defeated less people, impossible, since every one won at least a game.

stem_md: Show that  $ 2005^{2005}$  is a sum of two perfect squares, but not a sum of two perfect cubes.
solution_md:
Show that $ 2005^{2005}$ is a sum of two perfect squares, but not a sum of two perfect cubes.
$ 2005\equal{}41^2\plus{}18^2 \Rightarrow 2005^{2005}\equal{}(41 \times 2005^{1002})^2\plus{}(18 \times 2005^{1002})^2$ $ x^3 \equiv \minus{}1,0,1 \pmod{7}$ for all integer $ x$ $ \Rightarrow x^3\plus{}y^3 \equiv \minus{}2,\minus{}1,\minus{},1,2 \pmod{7}$ for all integers $ x$ and $ y$ But $ 2005 \equiv 1 \pmod{6} \Rightarrow 2005^{2005} \equiv 2005^{1} \equiv 3 \pmod{7}$ So $ 2005^{2005}$ cannot be sum of two perfect cubes, done.

stem_md: Let  $ D,E$  and  $ F$  be points on the sides  $ BC,CA$  and  $ AB$  respectively of a triangle  $ ABC$ , distinct from the vertices, such that  $ AD,BE$  and  $ CF$  meet at a point  $ G$ . Prove that if the angles  $ AGE,CGD,BGF$  have equal area, then  $ G$  is the centroid of  $ \triangle ABC$ .
solution_md:
I think the problem must be:
The triangles  $ AGE,CGD,BGF$  have the equal area.

Here is my solution:
Denote  $ x \equal{} S_{AGB},y \equal{} S_{BGC},z \equal{} S_{CGA}$ . We need to prove that  $ x \equal{} y \equal{} z$ 

Since  $ S_{AGE} \equal{} S_{AGC}.\frac{AE}{AC}$   $ S_{CGD} \equal{} S_{CGA}.\frac{GD}{GA}$  and  $ S_{AGE} \equal{} S_{CGD}$ , which implies  $ \frac{AE}{AC} \equal{} \frac{GD}{GA}$ 

By the other hand: $ \frac{AE}{AC} \equal{} \frac{S_{AGE}}{S_{AGC}} \equal{} \frac{S_{ABE}}{S_{ABC}} \equal{} \frac{S_{ABE} \minus{} S_{AGE}}{S_{ABC} \minus{} S_{AGC}} \equal{} \frac{S_{AGB}}{S_{AGB} \plus{} S_{BGC}} \equal{} \frac{x}{x \plus{} y}$ 
 $ \frac{GD}{GA} \equal{} \frac{S_{BGC}}{S_{AGB} \plus{} S_{CGA}} \equal{} \frac{y}{z \plus{} x}$ ,

which implies  $ \frac{x}{x \plus{} y} \equal{} \frac{y}{z \plus{} x}$ , $ (x \minus{} y)(x \plus{} y) \equal{} x(y \minus{} z)$ 

Similarity we obtain the system of equations: $ (x \minus{} y)(x \plus{} y) \equal{} x(y \minus{} z)$  $ (y \minus{} z)(y \plus{} z) \equal{} y(z \minus{} x)$  $ (z \minus{} x)(z \plus{} x) \equal{} z(x \minus{} y)$ 

If  $ x \equal{} y$ , we can easily solve the problem. Assume that  $ x,y,z$  are different, multiply three equations yields $ (x \plus{} y)(y \plus{} z)(z \plus{} x) \equal{} xyz$ , which is obviously wrong.

So  $ x \equal{} y \equal{} z$ , which implies  $ G$  is the centroid of triangle  $ ABC$

solution_md:
Let  $ ABC$  be a triangle and  $ G$  its centroid.

Using the triangle inequality we have  $ GB\plus{}GC>a\ \Longleftrightarrow m_b\plus{}m_c>\frac{3}{2}a$  and similarly  $ m_a\plus{}m_b>\frac{3}{2}c,\ m_a\plus{}m_c>\frac{3}{2}b$ . 
Summing up these inequalities we obtain the conclusion:  $ m_a\plus{}m_b\plus{}m_c>\frac{3}{4}(a\plus{}b\plus{}c)$

stem_md: Determine the number of arrangements  $ a_1,a_2,...,a_{10}$  of the numbers  $ 1,2,...,10$  such that  $ a_i>a_{2i}$  for  $ 1 \le i \le 5$  and  $ a_i>a_{2i\plus{}1}$  for  $ 1 \le i \le 4$ .
solution_md:
$ a_1>a_2,a_3$  $ a_2>a_4,a_5$  $ a_3>a_6,a_7$  $ a_4>a_8,a_9$  $ a_5>a_{10}$ 

Therefore  $ a_1\equal{}\max\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{10}\}\equal{}10$ . Note that the two subsets  $ \{a_2,a_4,a_5,a_8,a_9,a_{10}\}$  and  $ \{a_3,a_6,a_7\}$  do not affect each other. The number of possible distributions of 1,2,3,...,9 into these subsets is  $ \binom{9}3\equal{}63$ .

Now consider  $ a_2,a_4,a_5,a_8,a_9,a_{10}$ .  $ a_2$  is clearly the greatest. As before,  $ (a_4,a_8,a_9)$  and  $ (a_5,a_{10})$  do not affect each other, so there are  $ \binom53\equal{}10$  arrangements. But  $ a_8$  and  $ a_9$  are interchangeable, so this makes two arrangements. Now we have  $ 63\times10\times2\equal{}1260$  arrangements.

Lastly, consider  $ a_3,a_6,a_7$ .  $ a_3$  is the greatest, but  $ a_6$  and  $ a_7$  are interchangeable. So the total number of arrangements is  $ 1260\times2\equal{}2520$ .

stem_md: Let  $ x$  be an integer and  $ y,z,w$  be odd positive integers. Prove that  $ 17$  divides  $ x^{y^{z^w}}\minus{}x^{y^z}$ .
solution_md:
Let $ x$ be an integer and $ y,z,w$ be odd positive integers. Prove that $ 17$ divides $ x^{y^{z^w}} \minus{} x^{y^z}$ .
If $ 17|x$ then we are done. If not, then $ w \equiv 1 \pmod{2} \Rightarrow z^w \equiv z \pmod{4} \Rightarrow y^{z^w} \equiv y^z \pmod{16}$ $ \Rightarrow x^{y^{z^w}} \equiv x^{y^z} \pmod{17}$ by Fermat's little theorem. $ \Rightarrow 17|x^{y^{z^w}} \minus{} x^{y^z}$ , done also.

stem_md: Suppose that  $ m$  and  $ n$  are odd integers such that  $ m^2\minus{}n^2\plus{}1$  divides  $ n^2\minus{}1$ . Prove that  $ m^2\minus{}n^2\plus{}1$  is a perfect square.
solution_md:
Let's nail this guy (as far as I remember the original version involved also  $m>n>1$  condition). 

The idea is to set  $a=\frac{m+n}{2}$ ,  $b=\frac{m-n}{2}$  (hence  $a>0$  and  $b\ge 0$ ), and apply Vieta jumping. Specifically, after the aforementioned parameterization, it boils down  $4ab+1\mid (a-b)^2-1 \implies 4ab+1\mid (a+b)^2$ . To show  $4ab+1$  is a perfect square, it clearly suffices to show whenever  $4ab+1\mid (a+b)^2$ , it is the case that  $\frac{(a+b)^2}{4ab+1}$  is a perfect square. 

Define the set
\[
S=\left\{k:k=\frac{a^2+b^2}{4ab+1}\quad\text{for some}\quad a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\right\}.
\]
Take any  $k_0\in S$ , and let  $(a_0,b_0)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$  be a pair `realizing'  $k_0$  with the smallest  $a_0+b_0$  sum. Clearly if  $a_0=b_0$  then  $k_0=0$ , in which case we have the result. Assume  $a_0>b_0$  without loss of generality. Interpreting this condition as a quadratic in  $a$ , we arrive at
\[
a^2-a\left(4k_0b_0-2b_0\right)+b_0^2-k_0=0
\]
where the roots are  $a_0$  and  $\overline{a}$ . From Vieta's relations;
\[
a_0+ \overline{a} = b_0(4k_0-2) \quad\text{and}\quad a_0\overline{a} = b_0^2-k_0.
\]
It is evident, from the first condition, that  $\overline{a}$  is integral. Moreover, the pair  $(\overline{a},b_0)$  also realizes  $k_0$ . Now, if  $\overline{a} =0$  we immediately have  $k_0=b_0^2$ . Assume  $\overline{a}\ne 0$ . In order not to have a contradiction with the minimality of  $(a_0,b_0)$ , one of the two cases should be valid.**Case 1.**  $\overline{a}<0$ . In this case  $a_0|\overline{a}| = k_0-b_0^2>0$ . Moreover,  $a_0 >b_0(4k-2)$ . Since  $a_0\mid k_0-b_0^2$ , this yields  $b_0(4k_0-2)\le k-b^2$ . It is evident that in this case  $4kb_0+b_0^2-2b_0\le k$ . If  $b_0=0$ , we have the condition, if  $b_0=1$  we have  $4k-1\le k$ , forcing  $k=0$ ; whereas for  $b_0\ge 2$ , we have a contradiction. Case  $1$  is closed.**Case 2.** Now assume  $\overline{a}>0$ . In this case, since  $(a_0,b_0)$  realizes  $k_0$  with smallest  $a_0+b_0$ , it is the case that  $\overline{a}\ge a_0$ . Hence,  $b_0^2-k_0 =a_0\overline{a}\ge a_0^2$ . As  $a_0>b_0$  (by the choice) this is impossible.

Since  $k_0$  was arbitrary, the proof is finished.

stem_md: Are there integers  $x,y$  and  $z$  which satisfy the equation   $$ z^2=(x+1)(y^2-1)+n $$   when (a)  $n=2006$  (b)  $n=2007$ ?
solution_md:
Solution**Part (a).** We have  $$ z^2 = (x^2 + 1)(y^2 - 1) + n \implies z^2 - x^2y^2 + x^2 - y^2 = 2006. $$  Setting  $z = xy$ , we can solve  $$ x^2 - y^2 = 2006 \implies (x + y)(x - y) = 2005, $$  and checking factor pairs gives  $(x, y, z) = (203, 198, 40194)$  as a solution, so there are integers  $x, y, z$ .**Part (b)**. We note  $z^2 \equiv 0, 1,$  or  $4\pmod{8}$ .
Then  $(x^2 + 1) \equiv 1, 2,$  or  $5 \pmod{8}$ ,  $(y^2 - 1) \equiv 7, 0,$  or  $3 \pmod{8}$ , and  $2007 \equiv 7 \pmod{8}$ . Thus the RHS must be  $2, 5, 6$  or  $7 \pmod{8}$ , so there must be no solutions.

I claim that if  $m$  or  $n$  is odd, the person can escape.

Assume one of  $m, n$  is odd. It's easy to find a path for the person to take; just "snake" along, filling one column at a time.

Now, we prove that it is impossible for the person to succeed if  $m$  and  $n$  are both even. Let  $(m, n)$  refer to the room on the mth column and nth row.

Lemma: If  $m$  and  $n$  are the same parity, all paths from the beginning point to the end point cover an odd number of rooms, including the beginning and end rooms. Otherwise, all paths from the beginning point to the end point cover and even number of rooms.

We use induction. The base cases are trivial; we can find that a  $1$  by  $2k$  building always covers an even number of  rooms in a path, and a path on a  $1$  by  $2k+1$  always covers an odd number of rooms. 

Now, assume that this is true for all pairs  $(a, b)$  such that  $a\le m$  and  $b\le n$  except for the pair  $(m, n)$ . Now, to get to the room  $(m, n)$ , a path must go through one of these rooms directly before reaching  $(m, n)$ . This means that the parity of  $(m, n)$  is opposite the parity of  $(m-1, n)$ , which leads to the conclusion.

With this, the problem becomes very easy. When  $m$  and  $n$  are both even, every path goes through an odd number of rooms, but the total number of rooms is even, which means it's impossible for the person to legally traverse all of the rooms in the path.

WLOG let  $m$  be odd. To escape, go along the rows. You will change direction as you go from one row to another, so you will be going the same direction ( $m - 1$  changes) at the top row, and thus you will have been able to visit every room.

Now assume that  $m$  and  $n$  are even. Colour the grid in a chessboard-like-pattern. The number of black squares and white squares are equal as  $m$  and  $n$  are even. We note that the start and finish squares are the same colour (consider a 2x2 grid, repeatedly tiled, and bottom left and top right squares are the same colour). Every square visited is a different colour, and there is an even number of squares, so you must visit  $m \times n - 1$  rooms, so when you visit all of them, you must be in a different coloured room to the one you started in. Thus you can't finish in the top right as it's the same colour, so you cannot escape if both  $m$  and  $n$  are even.
(Similar argument to that from before but a little bit more visual using a checkerboard pattern rather than a parity argument. Fundamentally the same)

stem_md:
let x,y are positive and  $ \in R$  that :  $ x\plus{}2y\equal{}1$ .prove that :
\[ \frac{1}{x}\plus{}\frac{2}{y} \geq \frac{25}{1\plus{}48xy^2}\]
solution_md:
let x,y are positive and $ \in R$ that : $ x \plus{} 2y \equal{} 1$ .prove that : \[ \frac {1}{x} \plus{} \frac {2}{y} \geq \frac {25}{1 \plus{} 48xy^2} \]
It seems like it holds for all $ x,y \neq 0$ . Multiply with $ xy(1 \plus{} 48xy^2)$ and get: $ (y \plus{} 2x)(1 \plus{} 48xy^2) \ge 25xy$ $ \iff$ $ y \plus{} 2x \plus{} 48xy^3 \plus{} 96x^2y^2 \ge 25xy$ . Homogenizing: $ (y \plus{} 2x)(x \plus{} 2y)^3 \plus{} 48xy^3 \plus{} 96x^2y^2 \ge 25xy(x \plus{} 2y)^2$ $ \iff$ $ x^4 \plus{} 4y^4 \plus{} 13x^2y^2 \ge 6x^3y \plus{} 12xy^3$ . Set $ x \equal{} \sqrt {2}z$ . Then $ 4z^4 \plus{} 4y^4 \plus{} 26z^2y^2 \ge 12\sqrt {2}z^3y \plus{} 12\sqrt {2}zy^3$ . $ \iff$ $ 2z^4 \plus{} 2y^4 \plus{} 13z^2y^2 \ge 6\sqrt {2}z^3y \plus{} 6\sqrt {2}yz^3$ . Let $ f(y,z) \equal{} 2y^4 \plus{} 2z^4 \plus{} 13y^2z^2 \minus{} 6\sqrt {2}yz^3 \minus{} 6\sqrt {2}y^3z$ . Let $ z \equal{} 1$ .. $ f(y,1) \equal{} 2y^4 \minus{} 6\sqrt {2}y^3 \plus{} 13y^2 \minus{} 6\sqrt {2}y \plus{} 2$ . And this is a symmertric polynomial! (And these one can be factored, so we are on the rigth path! :) ) Since $ y,z \neq 0$ we have: $ f(y,z) \equal{} y^2z^2( 2(\frac {y}{z} \plus{} \frac {z}{y})^2 \minus{} 6\sqrt {2}(\frac {y}{z} \plus{} \frac {z}{y}) \plus{} 9)$ . Let $ w \equal{} \frac {y}{z} \plus{} \frac {z}{y}$ Then we just have to prove: $ 2w^2 \plus{} 9 \ge 6\sqrt {2}w$ , which follows directly from AM-GM. With equality iff $ w \equal{} 3$ $ \iff$ $ y \equal{} 2z$ or $ 2y \equal{} z$ . Done ^^

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer.
Find the greatest common divisor of the numbers  $\binom{2n}{1},\binom{2n}{3},\binom{2n}{5},...,\binom{2n}{2n-1}$ .
solution_md:
BISHAL_DEB how is that relevant? 

Consider an odd prime  $p|n$  such that it divides all the binomial coefficients. Write  $2n = b_1b_2...b_m$  in base  $p$ .
Then consider the number  $k = a_1a_2...a_m$  in base  $p$  such that  $a_i = 0$  whenever  $b_i = 0$  and  $a_i = 1$  otherwise. Then by Lucas's Theorem we have  $\dbinom{2n}{k} \not \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ , a contradiction unless  $k$  is even. But then change some non-zero  $a_j = 1$  into  $a_j = 0$  and we have  $k$  odd while  $\dbinom{2n}{k} \not \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$  and  $k$  is odd now, contradiction and hence no odd primes  $p$  divide all the binomial coefficients.

Now we determine the number of times two divides all the coefficients. I claim  $2^{v_2(2n)}$  divides all of the terms. Remark that if this is true, it is the maximum number of times because that's the highest power of  $2$  that divides  $\dbinom{2n}{1}$ To prove this, write  $\dbinom{2n}{m} = \frac{2n}{m} \cdot (\text{some integer})$  where  $m$  is odd. $v_2(\text{some integer}) \ge 0$  and  $v_2(2n/m) = v_2(2n)$ , hence  $2^{v_2(2n)}$  divides the binomial coefficient and hence the gcd is simply  $2^{v_2(2n)}$ .

stem_md: The point  $ P$  is a fixed point on a circle and  $ Q$  is a fixed point on a line. The point  $ R$  is a variable point on the circle such that  $ P,Q,$  and  $ R$  are not collinear. The circle through  $ P,Q,$  and  $ R$  meets the line again at  $ V$ . Show that the line  $ VR$  passes through a fixed point.
solution_md: Let  $ l$  be the fixed line and  $ \mathcal K$  the fixed circle. Inversion with center  $ P$  and arbitraty power takes  $ l$  into a fixed circle  $ \mathcal L'$  through  $ P$  and  $ \mathcal K$  through  $ P$  into a fixed line  $ k'.$  The fixed point  $ Q \in l$  goes to a fixed point  $ Q' \in \mathcal L'$  and the variable point  $ R \in \mathcal K$  goes to a variable point  $ R' \in k'.$   Circumcircle  $ \odot(PQR)$  goes to the line  $ Q'R'$  cutting  $ \mathcal L'$  again at the image  $ V'$  of  $ V,$  and line  $ VR$  goes to the circumcircle  $ \odot (PV'R').$  Let  $ S$  be its center.  $ \angle PSR' \equal{} 2 \angle PV'R' \equal{} 2 \angle PV'Q' \equal{} \text{const}$   $ \Longrightarrow$  the isosceles triangle  $ \triangle PSR'$  with the fixed vertex  $ P$  and  $ R' \in k'$  remains similar for all  $ R' \in k'$   $ \Longrightarrow$  locus of  $ S$  is a fixed line  $ s$   $ \Longrightarrow$  circles  $ \odot (PV'R')$  intersecting at  $ P$  form a pencil, they also intersect at the reflection  $ W'$  of  $ P$  in  $ s$   $ \Longrightarrow$  lines  $ VR$  go through the fixed image  $ W$  of  $ W'.$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Ireland Contests/Ireland National Math Olympiad/2007 Irish Math Olympiad/287213.json

The line  $ VR$  goes through the fixed point  $ S$

stem_md:
Let  $ r$  and  $ n$  be nonnegative integers such that  $ r \le n$ . 
 $ (a)$  Prove that:  $ \frac{n\plus{}1\minus{}2r}{n\plus{}1\minus{}r} \binom{n}{r}$  is an integer. 
 $ (b)$  Prove that:  $ \displaystyle\sum_{r\equal{}0}^{[n/2]}\frac{n\plus{}1\minus{}2r}{n\plus{}1\minus{}r} \binom{n}{r}<2^{n\minus{}2}$  for all  $ n \ge 9$ .
solution_md:
I will use 2 known identities:

(1)  $ \binom{n}{r} \equal{} \frac {n}{r}\binom{n \minus{} 1}{r \minus{} 1}$ 

(2)  $ \binom{n \plus{} 1}{r} \equal{} \binom{n}{r} \plus{} \binom{n}{r \minus{} 1}$ 

Proof (a):
 $ A \equal{} \frac {n \plus{} 1 \minus{} 2r}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r}\binom{n}{r} \equal{} \frac {n \plus{} 1}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r}\binom{n}{n \minus{} r} \minus{} \frac {2r}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r}\binom{n}{r}$ 

from (1) we can write
 $ \frac {n \plus{} 1}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r}\binom{n}{n \minus{} r} \equal{} \binom{n \plus{} 1}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r} \equal{} \binom{n \plus{} 1}{r}$ 

and
 $ \frac {2r}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r}\binom{n}{r} \equal{} \frac {2n}{n \plus{} 1 \minus{} r}\binom{n \minus{} 1}{r \minus{} 1} \equal{} 2\binom{n}{r \minus{} 1}$ 

now, from (2)  $ A$  become:
 $ A \equal{} \binom{n \plus{} 1}{r} \minus{} \binom{n}{r \minus{} 1} \minus{} \binom{n}{r \minus{} 1} \equal{} \binom{n}{r} \minus{} \binom{n}{r \minus{} 1} \Rightarrow$  A is an integer

Proof (b):

If we replace  $ A$  in the argument of the sum, we obtain:
 $ \sum_{r \equal{} 0}^{[n/2]}\left[\binom{n}{r} \minus{} \binom{n}{r \minus{} 1}\right] \equal{} \binom{n}{[n/2]}.$ 

Wow! And now ?

If we try with  $ n \equal{} 9$ , we obtain
 $ \binom{9}{4} \equal{} 126 < 2^7 \equal{} 128$   OK !

We can use a known result:

(3)  $ \binom{2n}{n} \leq \frac {4^n}{\sqrt {3n \plus{} 1}}$  for all  $ n\geq 1$ 

See here: [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_binomial_coefficient](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_binomial_coefficient)

Then it's easy now, because from (3):
 $ \binom{n}{[n/2]} < \frac {2^n}{\sqrt {3[n/2] \plus{} 1}} \leq \frac {2^n}{4}$  for all  $ n \geq 10$ , infact when  $ n \equal{} 10$  the identities hold:  $ \sqrt {3[10/2] \plus{} 1} \equal{} 4$ 
 $ \hfill{\square}$

Determine the value of:  $ \frac{r\minus{}1}{r\plus{}1}\plus{}\frac{s\minus{}1}{s\plus{}1}\plus{}\frac{t\minus{}1}{t\plus{}1}$ .
solution_md: Assume the roots of the equation  $x^3-2007x+2002=0$  are  $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$  By TOR we get,   $$ \frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+1}=t\implies\boxed{\alpha=\frac{t+1}{1-t}} $$   putting thus value on given equation we get,   $$ \left(\frac{t+1}{1-t}\right)^3-2007\left(\frac{t+1}{1-t}\right)+2002=0 $$     $$ \implies(t+1)^3-2007(1-t)^2(t+1)+2002=0\implies\boxed{2006t^3-2010t^2-2010t+4=0} $$   Therefore we get,   $$ \sum_{cyc}{}\left(\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+1}\right)=\frac{1005}{1003} $$  Vieta's Relation!!!! :love:

stem_md:
Suppose that  $ a,b,$  and  $ c$  are positive real numbers. Prove that:
 $ \frac{a\plus{}b\plus{}c}{3} \le \sqrt{\frac{a^2\plus{}b^2\plus{}c^2}{3}} \le \frac {\frac{ab}{c}\plus{}\frac{bc}{a}\plus{}\frac{ca}{b}}{3}$ .

solution_md: By AM-QM:  $\frac{a+b+c}{3} \le \sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{3}}$ Now, Consider the sequences  $(4,2,2),(4,4,0)$ .Then:  $ (4,2,2)\prec (4,4,0)$ By Muirhead’s theorem we obtain:  $T [4,2,2] \leq T [4,4,0]$  $\implies a^4b^2c^2+a^2b^4c^2+a^2b^2c^4 \leq a^4b^4+b^4c^4+c^4a^4$  $\implies a^2+b^2+c^2 \leq \frac{a^2b^2}{c^2}+\frac{b^2c^2}{a^2}+\frac{c^2a^2}{b^2}$ This is equivalent to: $ \sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{3}} \le \frac {\frac{ab}{c}+\frac{bc}{a}+\frac{ca}{b}}{3}$

stem_md: Determine, with proof, all integers  $ x$  for which  $ x(x\plus{}1)(x\plus{}7)(x\plus{}8)$  is a perfect square.
solution_md:
Let  $ u\equal{}x\plus{}4$ . This transforms the product into  $ (u\plus{}3)(u\minus{}3)(u\plus{}4)(u\minus{}4)\equal{}(u^2\minus{}9)(u^2\minus{}16)$ .
Now let  $ v\equal{}u^2\minus{}12$ . Then we have  $ (u^2\minus{}9)(u^2\minus{}16)\equal{}(v\minus{}4)(v\plus{}4\minus{}1)\equal{}(v^2\minus{}16)\minus{}(v\minus{}4)\equal{}v^2\minus{}v\minus{}12$ . This will be between  $ (v\minus{}1)^2$  and  $ v^2$  if  $ v> 13$ . We have  $ v\equal{}u^2\minus{}12\equal{}(x\plus{}4)^2\minus{}12$  so  $ v>13$  if  $ x>1$  or  $ x<\minus{}9$ . The cases of x in between are dealt with by brute force so  $ x\equal{}1,0,\minus{}1,\minus{}4,\minus{}7,\minus{}8,\minus{}9$

stem_md:
Suppose that  $ x, y$  and  $ z$  are positive real numbers such that  $ xyz \ge 1$ .

(a) Prove that $ 27 \le (1 \plus{} x \plus{} y)^2 \plus{} (1\plus{} x \plus{} z)^2 \plus{} (1 \plus{} y \plus{} z)^2$ ,
with equality if and only if  $ x \equal{} y \equal{} z \equal{} 1$ .

(b) Prove that $ (1 \plus{} x \plus{} y)^2 \plus{} (1\plus{} x \plus{} z)^2 \plus{} (1 \plus{} y \plus{} z)^2$   $ \le 3(x \plus{} y \plus{} z)^2$ ,
with equality if and only if  $ x \equal{} y \equal{} z \equal{} 1$ .
solution_md:
Suppose that $ x, y$ and $ z$ are positive real numbers such that $ xyz \ge 1$ . (b) Prove that $ (1 \plus{} x \plus{} y)^2 \plus{} (1 \plus{} x \plus{} z)^2 \plus{} (1 \plus{} y \plus{} z)^2$ $ \le 3(x \plus{} y \plus{} z)^2$ , with equality if and only if $ x \equal{} y \equal{} z \equal{} 1$ .
We can rewrite this ineq that: $ x^2\plus{}y^2\plus{}x^2\plus{}4(xy\plus{}yz\plus{}xz) \geq 4(x\plus{}y\plus{}z)\plus{}3$ Put $ f(x;y;z)\equal{}x^2\plus{}y^2\plus{}x^2\plus{}4(xy\plus{}yz\plus{}xz) \minus{} 4(x\plus{}y\plus{}z)\minus{}3$ Suppose that $ z\equal{}max{x;y;z}$ then $ z \geq 1$ and $ xy \geq \frac{1}{z}$ We have $ f(x;y;z)\minus{}f(\sqrt{xy};\sqrt{xy};z)\equal{}(x\minus{}y)^2\plus{}4(\sqrt{x}\minus{}\sqrt{y})^2(z\minus{}1) \geq 0$ Note that $ f(\sqrt{xy};\sqrt{xy};z)\equal{}6xy\plus{}8z\sqrt{xy}\minus{}8\sqrt{xy}\plus{}z^2\minus{}4z\minus{}3$ $ \geq \frac{6}{z}\plus{}8.\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}(z\minus{}1)\plus{}z^2\minus{}4z\minus{}3$ => $ zf(\sqrt{xy};\sqrt{xy};z)\equal{}(z\minus{}1)(\sqrt{z}\minus{}1)(z\sqrt{z}\plus{}z\minus{}2\sqrt{z}\plus{}6) \geq 0$ So we have $ f(x;y;z) \geq 0$ Equality occurs when $ x\equal{}y\equal{}z\equal{}1$

stem_md: Find all positive integers  $n$  for which  $n^8+n+1$  is a prime number.
solution_md:
Find all positive integers $n$ for which $n^8+n+1$ is a prime number.
Note that $n^8+n+1=(n^2+n+1)(n^6-n^5+n^3-n^2+1)$ , so we must have $n^6-n^5+n^3-n^2+1=1 \implies n^2(n^2+n+1)(n-1)^2=0$ , so $n=1$ . Verifying, we get $n^8+n+1=3$ , which is prime. Thus, $n=1$ is the only solution.

stem_md: Given an  $n$ -tuple of numbers  $(x_1,x_2,\dots ,x_n)$  where each  $x_i=+1$  or  $-1$ , form a new  $n$ -tuple   $$ (x_1x_2,x_2x_3,x_3x_4,\dots ,x_nx_1), $$  and continue to repeat this operation. Show that if  $n=2^k$  for some integer  $k\ge 1$ , then after a certain number of repetitions of the operation, we obtain the  $n$ -tuple   $$ (1,1,1,\dots ,1). $$
solution_md:
Thanks to **ThatApollo777** for spotting a huge error in my proof.**Setup: **Replace $\{1,-1\}$ by $\{0,1\}$ and addition modulo $2$ . For any tuple $S$ , let $f(S)$ denote the result of applying this operation on that tuple. We want to show eventually everything ends up at the zero tuple. The main point is that $f(A+B)=f(A)+f(B)$ , where addition is standard vector addition. Thus if we consider the $n$ "unit vectors" of the form $$ (0,\dots, 0, 1, 0, \dots, 0) $$ it suffices to show that each one of them eventually map to all 0s. Note that since this operation is cyclic, the process on each of the $n$ unit vectors is exactly the same up to a cyclic shift, so I show the claim for $(1,0,\dots, 0)$ . Infact, I show something stronger. I show that we can reach $$ (1,0, \dots 0)\rightarrow (0,\dots 0) $$ if and only if $n$ is a power of $2$ . For each position vector $v=(v_0, v_1, \dots v_{n-1})\in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ , consider the polynomial $$ f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}v_jx^j\in \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^n-1). $$ The key point is that in every stage, we multiply the polynomial by $1+x$ as the $x_i$ coefficient gets replaced by the sum of $x^{i}$ and $x^{i+1}$ coefficients. Thus our polynomial after $t$ steps becomes $$ f_t(x)=f(x)\cdot (1+x)^t\pmod{x^n-1}. $$ **Powers of 2: **Say $n=2^k$ for some positive integer $k$ . Note that for nonnegative integers $i$ , we have $$ (1+x)^{2^i}\equiv 1+x^{2^i} $$ in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ . Indeed, expanding and using Lucas theorem, since all intermediate binomial coefficients for powers of $2$ are even. Now in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^n-1)$ , we get $$ (1+x)^n\equiv 1+x^n\equiv 2\equiv 0 $$ so this shows that after $n$ steps, we reach all zeros, as desired. **Non powers of 2**: Say $$ (1+x)^t\equiv 0\in \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^n-1). $$ Consider a odd prime divisor $p$ of $n$ . We can work in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^p-1)$ . Pick a primitive $p$ th root in an extension of $\mathbb{F}_2$ . Say this is $\zeta$ . Some work(noting that $p$ is odd), can give us that $\zeta=1$ , but that contradicts that its a primitive root. This finishes.
RemarkThere are many elementary ways to execute the solution without generating functions. My first proof that $2^k$ works was quite elementary, but I couldnt find an elementary proof that non powers of two work and when I found the proof with genfunc, i realised that you can show powers of two work with pure gen func which I thought was cool. I saw this problem on an RMO mock, so for that purpose, this solution isnt the best one.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Ireland Contests/Ireland National Math Olympiad/2009 Irish Math Olympiad/1583276.json

In the triangle  $ABC$  we have  $|AB|<|AC|$ . The bisectors of the angles at  $B$  and  $C$  meet  $AC$  and  $AB$  at  $D$  and  $E$  respectively.  $BD$  and  $CE$  intersect at the incenter  $I$  of  $\triangle ABC$ .

Prove that  $\angle BAC=60^\circ$  if and only if  $|IE|=|ID|$
solution_md: If  $\angle BAC =60 \implies \angle BIC =120 \implies$  points  $A, E, I, D$  lie on the same circle  $\implies \angle EDI = \angle EAI = \angle DAI = \angle DEI \implies IE=ID$   $\blacksquare$ If  $IE=ID$ , we look at  $\triangle AEI$  and  $\triangle ADI$ . We have  $AI=AI$ ;  $\angle EAI= \angle DAI$ ;  $IE=ID$ , thus  $\angle AEI = \angle ADI$  or  $\angle AEI = 180 - \angle ADI$ . The first case does not work, because we get  $\triangle ADB \equiv AEC \implies AB=AC$ , contradiction. So,  $\angle AEI = 180 - \angle ADI \implies$  points  $A, E, I, D$  lie on the same circle  $\implies \angle BAC = 180 - \angle EID = 180 - \angle BIC = 180 - (90 + \frac{\angle BAC}{2}) \implies 3 \cdot \angle BAC = 180 \implies \angle BAC = 60$   $\blacksquare$

Hello.

Suppose  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  are real numbers such that  $a+b+c = 0$  and  $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} = 1$ .
Prove that  $a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}\leq \frac{1}{54}$  and determine the cases of equality.
solution_md:
Hello. Suppose $a$ , $b$ , $c$ are real numbers such that $a+b+c = 0$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} = 1$ . Prove that $a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}\leq \frac{1}{54}$ and determine the cases of equality.
$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} a + b + c = 0 a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1 \end{array} \right. \Rightarrow \left( {a + b} \right)^2 - ab = \frac{1}{2}$ so $a^2 b^2 c^2 = \left( {ab} \right)^2 \left( {a + b} \right)^2 = \left( {\left( {a + b} \right)^2 - \frac{1}{2}} \right)^2 \left( {a + b} \right)^2 = \frac{{t\left( {2t - 1} \right)^2 }}{4} = f\left( t \right)$ where $t = \left( {a + b} \right)^2 $ , and $\left( {a + b} \right)^2 - ab = \frac{1}{2} \Leftrightarrow \left( {a - b} \right)^2 + 3\left( {a + b} \right)^2 = 2 $ give $t \in \left[ {0,\frac{2}{3}} \right]$ so $f'\left( t \right) = \frac{{\left( {6t - 1} \right)\left( {2t - 1} \right)}}{4}$ $\Rightarrow f\left( t \right) \le \max \left\{ {f\left( {\frac{1}{6}} \right),f\left( {\frac{2}{3}} \right)} \right\} = \max \left\{ {\frac{1}{{54}},\frac{1}{{54}}} \right\} = \frac{1}{{54}}$ equality holds if any only if $t=\frac{1}{6}$ or $t=\frac{2}{3}$ , i.e. $(a+b)^2=\frac{1}{6}$ or $(a+b)^2=\frac{2}{3}$ , i.e. $\left\{ {a,b,c} \right\} = \left\{ {\frac{1}{{\sqrt 6 }},\frac{1}{{\sqrt 6 }}, - \frac{2}{{\sqrt 6 }}} \right\}$ or $\left\{ {a,b,c} \right\} = \left\{ { - \frac{1}{{\sqrt 6 }}, - \frac{1}{{\sqrt 6 }},\frac{2}{{\sqrt 6 }}} \right\}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $P(x)$  be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that there exists a positive integer  $n$  such that the polynomial  $Q(x)$  defined by
\[Q(x)= P(x+n)-P(x)\]
has integer coefficients.
solution_md:
We can write  $P(x) = \frac {1} {N} R(x)$  for some  $R(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  and positive integer  $N$  (by collecting denominators of the coefficients of  $P(x)$ ). 
Then  $Q(x) =  \frac {1} {N} (R(x+n) - R(x))$ .
Let  $R(x) = \sum_{j=0}^k a_jx^j$ , with  $a_j \in \mathbb{Z}$ . Then  $R(x+n) - R(x) = \sum_{j=0}^k a_j(x+n)^j - \sum_{j=0}^k a_jx^j = \sum_{j=0}^k a_jx^j + nS(x) - \sum_{j=0}^k a_jx^j = nS(x)$ , for some  $S(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ .
It is therefore enough to take  $n=N$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Ireland Contests/Ireland National Math Olympiad/2009 Irish Math Olympiad/461662.json

stem_md:
Hamilton Avenue has eight houses. On one side of the street are the houses
numbered 1,3,5,7 and directly opposite are houses 2,4,6,8 respectively. An
eccentric postman starts deliveries at house 1 and delivers letters to each of
the houses, finally returning to house 1 for a cup of tea. Throughout the
entire journey he must observe the following rules. The numbers of the houses
delivered to must follow an odd-even-odd-even pattern throughout, each house
except house 1 is visited exactly once (house 1 is visited twice) and the postman
at no time is allowed to cross the road to the house directly opposite. How

stem_md: Find the least  $k$  for which the number  $2010$  can be expressed as the sum of the squares of  $k$  integers.
solution_md: Assume that it can be written as the sum of 2 squares. Then,  $x^2 + y^2 = 2010  \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ . Since the quadratic residues mod  $3$  are just  $0$  and  $1$ , this means that  $x$  and  $y$  are both divisible by  $3$ . However, this is impossible because this would imply  $9 | (x^2 + y^2)$ . Therefore,  $k = 2$  is impossible. For  $k=3$ , we see that  $5^2 + 7^2 + 44^2 = 2010$ . Therefore,  $\boxed{k=3}$ .

stem_md: In triangle  $ABC$  we have  $|AB|=1$  and  $\angle ABC=120^\circ.$  The perpendicular line to  $AB$  at  $B$  meets  $AC$  at  $D$  such that  $|DC|=1$ . Find the length of  $AD$ .
solution_md:
Let  $BC=a$ From the sine rule on triangle  $BDC$   $$ \frac{a}{\sin\left(90+A\right)}=\frac{1}{\sin\left(30\right)}=2 $$    $$ \cos A=\frac{a}{2} $$  As  $ABD$  is right angled at  $B$   $$ AD\cos A=AB=1 $$    $$ AD=\frac{2}{a} $$  Using the cosine rule on triangle  $ABC$   $$ \frac{a^2+1-\left(\frac{2}{a}+1\right)^2}{2a}=\cos120=\frac{-1}{2} $$  Simplifying, we get  $$ a^4+a^3-4a-4=0 $$    $$ \left(a+1\right)\left(a^3-4\right)=0 $$  And so  $a\ =\ \sqrt[3]{4}$ , as  $a$  cannot be negative
Hence  $AD=\frac{2}{a}=\sqrt[3]{2}$

stem_md: Let  $n\ge 3$  be an integer and  $a_1,a_2,\dots ,a_n$  be a finite sequence of positive integers, such that, for  $k=2,3,\dots ,n$    $$ n(a_k+1)-(n-1)a_{k-1}=1. $$   Prove that  $a_n$  is not divisible by  $(n-1)^2$ .
solution_md:
ProofSolving in terms of $a_k$ , we find $a_k=\frac{(n-1)(a_{k-1}-1)}{n}$ By induction $$ a_k=\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{k-1}a_1-n\left(1-\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{k-1}\right)=(a_1+n)\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{k-1}-n $$ So when $k=n$ we find $$ a_n=(a_1+n)\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{n-1}-n\equiv -n\not\equiv 0\pmod{n-1} \blacksquare $$

stem_md: $ABCD$  is a rectangle.  $E$  is a point on  $AB$  between  $A$  and  $B$ , and  $F$  is a point on  $AD$  between  $A$  and  $D$ . solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $DF = a, DA = BC = x, EB = b, AB = DC = y$ . 
Then  $AF = x - a, AE = y- b$ . 
Note that we are looking for  $[EFC] = [ABCD] - 16 - 30 - 12 = [ABCD] - 58 = xy - 58$ .
Using the given information, we have the following equations:  $$ ay = 60 \quad (*) $$    $$ xb = 32 \quad (**) $$    $$ (x - a)(y - b) = xy - (ay + xb) + ab = 24 \quad (***) $$  Substituting  $(*), (**)$  into  $(***)$  gives  $xy + ab  = 24 + 92 = 116 \quad (****)$ .
Now multiply  $(*), (**)$  yielding  $xyab = 1920$ . 
We can rewrite this as  $ab = \frac{1920}{xy}$ .
Substitute into  $(****)$ , yielding  $xy + \frac{1920}{xy} = 116$ .
Rewrite the equation as  $(xy)^2 - 116xy + 1920 = 0$ , so we have  $(xy - 20)(xy - 96) = 0$ .
We cannot have  $xy = 20$  as  $16 + 12 + 30 = 58 > 20$ .
Thus  $xy = [ABCD] = 96$ .
Then  $[EFC] = 96 - 58 = 38$ .</details>

Proceeding as @2 above, if that expression were a natural, so is $$ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}...+\frac{1}{2011} $$ Now, making the denominator common, we get a numerator $N$ and a denomiantor $D$ . Note that the expression being natural forces $D\mid N$ . As $2011 \mid D , 2011\mid N$ . But using the fact that $2011$ is prime, and that in the numerator, all the terms except $3\cdot 5\cdot 7\dots 2009$ are divisible by $2011$ . For the first, simply observe that, with  $t=xy+yz+zx$ , basic AM-GM gives,  $t\geq 3(xyz)^{2/3}$ , hence,  $xyz\leq (t/3)^{3/2}$ . Therefore,  $$ 1=2xyz+xy+yz+zx \leq 2(t/3)^{3/2}+t. $$  Clearly,  $xy+yz+zx<1$ ; and for the other inequality, simply assume that it is false, and that,  $t<3/4$ , for at least one triple  $(x,y,z)$ , satisfying the inequality. Since the right-hand-side above is increasing in  $t$ , this would give,  $$ 1\leq 2(t/3)^{3/2}+t <\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{4}=1, $$  a contradiction.

For the inequality involving  $xyz$ , now, we have,  $1=2xyz+xy+yz+zx \geq 2xyz + 3(xyz)^{2/3}$ . Letting,  $xyz=k^3$ , we get,  $2k^3+3k^2 - 1 \leq 0 \implies (k+1)(2k^2+k-1)\leq 0\implies 2k^2+k-1\leq 0 \implies k \leq \frac{1}{2}$ . Hence,  $xyz\leq \frac{1}{8}$ .

For the last inequality, use,  $(x+y+z)^2\geq 3(xy+yz+zx) \geq \frac{9}{4}$ , and conclude.

stem_md:
The integers  $a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3,\ldots$  are defined as follows: $a_0 = 1$ ,  $a_1 = 3$ , and  $a_{n+1} = a_n + a_{n-1}$  for all  $n \ge 1$ .
Find all integers  $n \ge 1$  for which  $na_{n+1} + a_n$  and  $na_n + a_{n-1}$  share a common factor greater than  $1$ .
solution_md:
The recursive sequence  $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$  is defined as follows: $(1) \; a_{n+1} = a_n + a_{n-1} \; (n \geq 1)$ ,

where  $a_0=1$  and  $a_1=3$ .

For a fixed  $n$ , define  $(2) \; b_k=na_{k+1} + a_k \; (k \geq 0)$ .

Let  $d_n=GCD(b_n, b_{n-1})$ .  Then by (2) and (1) $d_n | b_n - b_{n-1} = na_{n+1} + a_n - (na_n + a_{n-1}) = n(a_{n+1} - a_n) + (a_n - a_{n-1}) = na_{n-1} + a_{n-2} = b_{n-2}$ .

Hence, by induction,  $d_n|b_k$  for all  $k \leq n+1$ . Thus  $d_n|b_0 = na_1 + a_0 = 3n+1$  and  $d_n|b_1=na_2 + a_1 = 4n + 3$ , implying $d_n|3b_1 - 4b_0 = 3(4n+3) - 4(3n+1) = 5$ .

In other words,  $d_n \in \{1,5\}$ . 

Now  $a_0 \equiv 1$ ,  $a_1 \equiv 3$ ,  $a_2 \equiv 4$ ,  $a_3 \equiv 2$ ,  $a_4 \equiv 1$ ,  $a_5 \equiv 3, \ldots$  modulo 5, yielding  $a_{k+4} \equiv a_k \pmod{5}$ ,  $(3) \; a_{k+1} \equiv 3a_k \pmod{5}$  

and  $(4) \; a_k \not \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ for all  $k \geq 0$ .  Therefore by (3) $(5) \; b_{k+1} = na_{k+1} + a_k \equiv 3na_k + a_k = (3n+1)a_k \pmod{5}$ .

Combining (5) and (4), the result is  $5 | b_{k+1} \;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\; 5 | (3n+1)a_k  \;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\; 5 | 3n+1 \;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\; 5 | n-3$ .

Combining this with  $d_n = GCD(b_n,b_{n-1}) \in \{1,5\}$ , we reach the following conclusion: $d_n = GCD(na_{n+1} + a_n,na_n + a_{n-1}) > 1 \;\;\; \Longleftrightarrow \:\;\; n \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$ .

stem_md: Let  $S(n)$  be the sum of the decimal digits of  $n$ . For example.  $S(2012)=2+0+1+2=5$ . Prove that there is no integer  $n>0$  for which  $n-S(n)=9990$ .
solution_md:
Clearly  $n\geq9990$ .  
If  $9990\leq{n}\leq9999$ , then  $S(n)$  is at least  $9+9+9$  or  $27$ , so it is obvious that  $n-S(n)$  is less than  $9990$ .
Also, if  $n$  has  $x$  digits in its decimal representation, then  $min[n-S(n)]\leq{10^x-9x}$ . This is an increasing function of  $x$  when  $x\in\mathbb{N}$ . So we see  $x\leq6$ . 
So  $x=5$  which implies  $n\leq{9990+9\times5}$  or  $n\leq10035$ . 
Thus,  $S(n)\leq{1+0+0+9+9}$   $\implies$   $S(n)\leq{19}$ . 
Therefore  $n\leq{9990+19}$  or  $n\leq{10009}$ .
So  $S(n)\leq{10}$  which means  $n\leq{9990+10}$ , i.e.,  $n\leq{10000}$ .  $n=10000$  gives no solution, so the equation  $n-S(n)=9990$  has no solutions.

stem_md: Find the smallest positive integer  $m$  such that  $5m$  is an exact 5th power,  $6m$  is an exact 6th power, and  $7m$  is an exact 7th power.
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>The only number we need to consider is the number of the form  $N=2^a3^b5^c7^d$ . Let's start by calculating the minimum value for  $a$ . We must have   $$ a\equiv0\pmod{5} $$    $$ a\equiv5\pmod{6} $$    $$ a\equiv0\pmod{7}. $$   Solving this system, the minimum value for  $a$  is  $a=35$ . The same conditions apply for  $b$ , so the minimum value for  $b$  is also  $b=35$ . For  $c$ , we must have   $$ c\equiv4\pmod{5} $$    $$ c\equiv0\pmod{6} $$    $$ c\equiv0\pmod{7}. $$   Solving this system, the minimum value for  $c$  is  $c=84$ . For  $d$ , we must have   $$ d\equiv0\pmod{5} $$    $$ d\equiv0\pmod{6} $$    $$ d\equiv6\pmod{7}. $$   Solving this final system, the minimum value for  $d$  is  $d=90$ . Therefore, the smallest number that satisfies the conditions of the problem is  $\boxed{N=2^{35}3^{35}5^{84}7^{90}}$ .</details>

stem_md: $A, B$  and  $C$  are points on the circumference of a circle with centre  $O$ . Tangents are drawn to the circumcircles of triangles  $OAB$  and  $OAC$  at  $P$  and  $Q$  respectively, where  $P$  and  $Q$  are diametrically opposite  $O$ . The two tangents intersect at  $K$ . The line  $CA$  meets the circumcircle of  $\triangle OAB$  at  $A$  and  $X$ . Prove that  $X$  lies on the line  $KO$ .
solution_md: Invert about (ABC). We want to show that if  $OK'$  meets  $A'B'$  at  $X'$ , then  $X'$  lies on the circle  $OC'X'A'$ . Angle chasing, we have  $$ \angle X'A'C' = \angle B'A'C' = \frac{1}{2} \angle B'OC', $$  so if  $\frac{1}{2}\angle B'OC' = X'OC'$  then we are done. This occurs if  $OK'$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $B'C'$ , so it suffices to show (since  $OB'C'$  is isosceles) that  $B'C' \perp OK'$ . We have  $K'Q'P'$  collinear and  $OK'$  perpendicular to  $P'Q'$ , since  $\angle OK'Q'$  and  $\angle OK'P'$  are right angles. Finally, if we consider the homothety at  $A$  with ratio  $2$ , this sends  $P'Q'$  to  $B'C'$  by midpoints, so  $P'Q'$  is parallel to  $B'C'$ , and thus  $B'C'$  is perpendicular to  $O'K'$  and we are done.

stem_md:
The three distinct points $ B, C, D$  are collinear with C between B and D. Another point A not on
the line BD is such that  $|AB| = |AC| = |CD|.$ Prove that ∠ $BAC = 36$  if and only if  $1/|CD|-1/|BD|=1/(|CD| + |BD|)$ .
solution_md:
The three distinct points $ B, C, D$ are collinear with C between B and D. Another point A not on the line BD is such that $|AB| = |AC| = |CD|.$ Prove that ∠ $BAC = 36$ if and only if $1/|CD|-1/|BD|=1/(|CD| + |BD|)$ .
****Suppose that we have: $\widehat{BAC}=\frac{\pi}{5}$ , and it is well-known that $\cos(\frac{\pi}{5})=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}$ . We also denote: $AB=AC=CD=a$ . By Alkashi formula's, we obtain: $BC^2=AB^2+AC^2-2.AB.AC.\cos(\widehat{BAC})=2a^2(1-\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4})$ . So $BC^2=2a^2(\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{4})=a^2(\frac{6-2\sqrt{5}}{2^2})=a^2.\frac{(\sqrt{5}-1)^2}{2^2}$ . Then $BC=a\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ . We conclude that: $BD=BC+CD=a\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}+a=a\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2}$ . We have: $\frac{1}{CD}-\frac{1}{BD}=\frac{1}{a}-\frac{2}{a.(\sqrt{5}+1)}=\frac{1}{a}(1-\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2})=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2})$ . And: $\frac{1}{CD+BD}=\frac{1}{a(1+\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2})}=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{2}{3+\sqrt{5}})=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2})$ . We are done! ****Now, if we have: $\frac{1}{CD}-\frac{1}{BD}=\frac{1}{BC+BD}$ . This condition is equivalent to $BC^2+a.BC-a^2=0$ with the same notation. We can consider it as an equation in $BC$ , and it's discriminent is $\Delta=a^2+4a^2=5a^2$ . Then, the equation has two solutions, and we reject the negative one. So, $BC=\frac{a+a\sqrt{5}}{2}=a.\frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ . We denote: $\widehat{BAC}=\alpha$ , we conclude $\widehat{ABC}=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{2}$ because $AB=AC=a$ . By the sinus law, we get: $\frac{\sin(\alpha)}{BC}=\frac{\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{2})}{a}$ so $\frac{2\sin(\frac{\alpha}{2}).\cos{(\frac{\alpha}{2})}}{a.\frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2}}=\frac{\cos(\frac{\alpha}{2})}{a}$ . Then, $\sin({\frac{\alpha}{2}})=\frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{4}$ . We have: $\cos{(\frac{\alpha}{2})}=\sqrt{1-(\frac{-1+sqrt{5}}{4})^2}=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{10+2\sqrt{5}}=\cos(\frac{\pi}{10})$ . So, $\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{\pi}{10}$ , and $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{5}$ . ****References: http://mathworld.wolfram.com/TrigonometryAnglesPi10.html and http://mathworld.wolfram.com/TrigonometryAnglesPi5.html .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Ireland Contests/Ireland National Math Olympiad/2013 Irish Math Olympiad/542541.json

segment BC. The three angles ∠BAD, ∠DAM and ∠MAC are all equal. Find the angles of the

solution_md:
Let the equal angles be  $x$ . Then  $BAM$  is isosceles and  $\angle B=90-x,$  and therefore  $\angle C=90-2x$ . Thus  $0<x<45^\circ$ . 

Now  $(BAM)=(MAC)$  and thus  $\frac{1}{2}\cdot c\cdot AM\cdot \sin (2x)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot AM\cdot \sin x$ ; therefore  $b=2c\sin x$ . But from the law of sines we have  $\frac{b}{\cos x}=\frac{c}{\cos 2x}$ . stem_md:
Over a period of  $k$  consecutive days, a total of  $2014$  babies were born in a certain city, with at least one baby being born each day. Show that:
(a) If  $1014 < k \le 2014$ , there must be a period of consecutive days during which exactly  $100$  babies were born.
(b) By contrast, if  $k = 1014$ , such a period might not exist.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $x_i$  refer to the cumulative number of babies born in the first  $i$  days. So we would have  $k+1$  distinct  $x_i$ , with  $x_0=0,\ x_k=2014$  etc. We want to show that if  $k\ge1015$  then there must be two  $x_i,\ x_j$  which differ by exactly  $100$ . We will use the pigeon hole principle. Consider the following sets: $\left\{0,\ 100,\ 200,\ ...\ ,\ 2000\right\}$  $\left\{1,\ 101,\ 201,\ ...\ ,\ 2001\right\}$ so just the numbers from  $0$  to  $2014$  mod  $100$ . The first  $15$  of these sets will have  $21$  elements and the remaining  $85$  will have  $20$ . Suppose that there are not two  $x_i,\ x_j$  which differ by exactly  $100$ . Then there can be at most  $11$   $x_i$  in the first  $15$  sets and  $10$   $x_i$  in the remaining  $85$  sets. So we get  $k+1\le\left(11\cdot15\right)+\left(10\cdot85\right)$  and thus  $k\le1014$ . 

For a counter example when  $k=1014$ , just have  $1$  child be born on day  $i$  if  $i$  is not a multiple of  $100$  and have  $101$  children be born on day  $i$  if  $i$  is a multiple of  $100$ , so we would get the set of  $x_i$  being  $\left\{0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ ...\ 99,\ 200,\ 201,\ 202,\ ...\ 299,\ 400,\ ...,\ 2000,\ 2001,\ ...\ 2014\right\}$</details>

Let  $g(x)$  denote the product  $(x + a_1)\cdot ... \cdot (x + a_n)$  . 
Let  $a_0$  be a real number and let $f(x) = (x - a_0)g(x)= x^{n+1} + b_1x^n + b_2x^{n-1}+...+ b_nx + b_{n+1}$  .

But  $s_{k+1}<s_1s_k$  is also obvious as all of the terms in the sum  $s_{k+1}$  appear in sum after opening brackets in  $s_1s_k$  which also have some positive terms.

stem_md: Three different non-zero real numbers  $a,b,c$  satisfy the equations  $a+\frac{2}{b}=b+\frac{2}{c}=c+\frac{2}{a}=p $ , where  $p$  is a real number. Prove that   $abc+2p=0.$
solution_md:
Eliminating  $b$  and  $c$  gives  $(p^2-2)(a^2-pa+2)=0$ .

If  $p\ne\pm\sqrt2$  then  $a=\frac{p\pm\sqrt{p^2-8}}2$  and substituting into  $c+\frac2a=p$  gives  $c=a$ . But we are given that  $a,b,c$  are distinct. Hence we must have  $p=\pm\sqrt2$ .

Then  $2=p^2=\left(a+\frac2b\right)\left(b+\frac2c\right)=ab+\frac{2a}c+\frac4{bc}+2$   $\implies$   $0=abc+2\left(a+\frac2b\right)=abc+2p$ .
